items.body: Across its seventeen tracks, Wahj brings together electronics, industrial textures, processed strings, Arabic vocal traditions and fractured rhythms in combinations that keep changing shape. Individual elements remain recognisable without settling into familiar forms, while images of voice, disappearance, radiance and return recur throughout the album. Wahj took shape over five years, and the events of that period inevitably entered the music. As Toni Geitani explains in the accompanying interview, the album was not initially conceived as a meditation on collapse. The idea emerged gradually as the circumstances surrounding its composition changed. Collapse here is not a single catastrophic moment. Ruin exists alongside what persists, with Geitani attentive to the lives and voices that political violence can obscure. This runs through the lyrics as well as the music. Voices appear and disappear, sometimes sounding like invocations, sometimes carrying fragments of collective memory. On the brief “Sawtuka”, Geitani repeats, “Raise your voice higher and higher. Even if they bind you, even if they take you through death, the echo of your voice will remain forever.” The refrain turns persistence itself into an act of resistance. “2092” projects the idea into an imagined future in which “every fascist has fallen, and their glory belongs to nothingness,” before asking, “Does love remain when everything has vanished?” “Hal”, “Ruwaydan Ruwaydan” and the extended instrumental closer “Madda Mudadda” draw on ritual, repetition and moments of ecstatic release, with their meanings left open. The title, Wahj, points towards radiance, although Geitani gives the word no easy redemptive meaning. Light appears amid destruction, sometimes faintly, and does not cancel what surrounds it. In “Tuyoor”, the image is carried by birds: “The birds flying above you do not belong to the ruler who oppressed you. They watch the sky, not the earth beneath you.” The image opens a space outside the authority of the ruler, even while that authority continues to shape life below. Throughout Wahj, Geitani keeps returning to such spaces: voices that outlast attempts to silence them, traces of love after disappearance, and forms of life that continue amid devastation. To discuss the making of Wahj, we approched Toni Geitani directly. Wahj is described as an album about collapse, but one that refuses to remain trapped within its concept. Across the record, images of ruin, mourning, exile, and disappearance are constantly accompanied by gestures toward radiance, return, and endurance. How did you approach balancing these opposing forces while writing the album? I didn’t start working on the album with any intention of a “theme”, in this case collapse. I also wasn’t trying to narrow down the album to one thematic focus. It was an intuitive process that mostly guided the work. But it is true that as the project developed over five years, a lot of horrific events unfolded; consecutively and sometimes simultaneously. This naturally affected the relation to my work in a way that pushed me into ending up with these tracks, which I could eventually describe as being about collapse. By saying that the album refuses to be reduced to collapse, I’m intentionally pushing back against the idea that collapse is only a sudden, singular catastrophe. I was born in the 1990s in post-civil-war Lebanon, so from early on I was surrounded by war stories told by family and friends. After continuous exposure to these stories throughout my life, I came to understand that they were not stories of the past only, but of a collapse that kept resurfacing in different forms. At the same time, however, I was also exposed to another image of collapse that dominated global media and felt especially present in my teens in the 2000s. It was that of an image imported from the West, romanticized, and flattened into spectacle. It also ignores how, for some populations, collapse is already ongoing rather than a problem of the future or an isolated incident that can be inherited and prolonged. That difference matters to me because, for many of us, imperialism, colonialism, and capitalism are not warnings of an apocalypse to come, but they morph to become ongoing and almost fixed conditions. So when I was writing Wahj, I didn’t feel that I was trying to balance opposing forces simply because I do not see them as opposing, but inevitably coexisting. Instead, I was trying to remain faithful to everything catastrophe-centered narratives tend to erase: memory, resistance, regeneration, and the human capacity to continue. They are what must be reclaimed from within it. The lyrics repeatedly return to voices, echoes, and acts of calling out across distance. In “Sawtuka” (“Your Voice”), for example, the refrain insists that a voice survives even imprisonment or death, while tracks like “2092” and “Tuyoor” are structured around questions of who is listening and who remains absent. What role does the voice play in Wahj—as memory, resistance, testimony, or something else entirely? For this album, I composed the music before writing the lyrics. I would often record a vocal melody, sometimes with words that made sense and sometimes not, simply to find a fitting flow and have it as a placeholder until the final vocal recording. But before I began writing and recording the lyrics, the genocide in Gaza began alongside the war on Lebanon in 2023, so I stopped working on the album because I felt uneasy about prioritizing it. At that point, nothing made sense anymore. But somehow, by the beginning of 2025, I found the motivation to finish the project, and thus the lyrics were written. In my opinion, the voice can hold many roles at once, including the ones mentioned in the question. It is not intended to be a tool for meaning-making, but rather a presence moving through space, carrying the emotional and political conditions of that space with it. However, its position is immanent rather than observational. It does not stand outside the world to explain it. Instead, it emerges from within that world and continually reaches outward, while refusing to die. The lyrics inevitably reflect the experience of witnessing a 24/7 livestreamed ongoing Palestinian genocide, and the rage, injustice, betrayal, pain, and constant aggression we have been dealing with for many years. However, I do not wish to limit the album’s interpretation to the events of the past three years. As I mentioned earlier, collapse is not a one-time event or a singular fall, but I insist that it emerges from an ongoing oppression imposed on us by the same death machine. Musically, the album moves between processed classical instruments, layālī-inspired vocal passages, industrial textures, dark ambient atmospheres, and fractured electronic rhythms without ever fully settling into any one genre. Did you begin with a clear sonic vision for Wahj, or did this hybrid language emerge gradually during the five years of recording between 2021 and 2025? I did begin with a fairly clear sonic vision for Wahj, in the sense that from the beginning I wanted it to explore different genres and subgenres while still remaining rooted in electronics. What emerged gradually was not that intention itself, but the specific language the album took on through time, collaboration, experimentation, and everything that happened across those years. After releasing my first album in 2018, I wanted to keep exploring and collaborating before putting out another record. Between 2018 and 2020, I performed many live shows in Lebanon, where improvisation became an important space for testing new ideas and compositions. Over time, this left me with more than a hundred sketches, from which I selected the ones that felt less attached to a single genre and more committed to a shared atmosphere and universe, even if that universe itself remains unstable and fluctuating. When I began my studies at the Conservatorium van Amsterdam in 2021, that process expanded further. Being surrounded by many different kinds of musicians pushed me to explore classical instrumentation, processing, and different digital approaches in ways I had not tried beforehand. I recorded many phrases and ideas with musicians there, often without knowing exactly what their final form would be, because part of the process was discovering how their playing could be transformed and absorbed into the album’s sonic world. In that sense, the hybrid language of the record was both intended and gradually revealed. As mentioned earlier, I returned to working on the album in the beginning of 2025, and that final period inevitably shaped the work in a profound way. So while the album’s sonic foundation was there from the beginning, its final form was shaped by a long process of experimentation, disruption, and response to the world it was being made within. Several tracks evoke futures rather than simply documenting the present. The title “2092,” in particular, imagines a distant horizon where “every fascist has fallen and their glory belongs to nothingness,” while love and memory continue to endure. What attracted you to speculative or future-oriented thinking as a way of responding to contemporary political realities? I would like to make a distinction between futurism as typically understood through a Eurocentric lens which is rooted in Euro-American frameworks and historically entangled with imperialism and fascism – and counterfuturism that emerged from the Global South which functions to complicate normalized notions of time and technology rather than projecting a single vision of the future. And this is precisely what I intend to convey in the practice of imagining futures in the album, which attempt to articulate a cultural politics of time and become a means of writing alternative histories that distance themselves from any established history already written. This could mean reclaiming the right to think beyond imperialist scripts through collective knowledge, agency, and world-making rather than celebrating rupture, domination, or heroic modernity. In other words, I’m trying to open possibilities from within collapse, and thus, this framework differs from futurism as an approach for technocratic future-thinking. For example in “2092”, I try to treat the future as a tool to ask whose futures have been denied or flattened, instead of assuming it operates in a single path of progress. The political visions I sing about are not predictions, but they gesture toward an intense need to imagine the aftermath of collapse in the hope that something promising might emerge from it. That being said, I don’t intend for my songs to be frontal or overly obvious in their interpretation, and I welcome listeners to bring different meanings to them. You wrote a master’s thesis titled Sampling as a Political Medium, examining questions of power, appropriation, and cultural memory. Wahj incorporates repurposed regional sounds and references while constructing an entirely new sonic language. How has your thinking about sampling evolved since that research, and how do those ideas inform the album’s relationship to Arabic musical traditions and collective memory? My thinking on sampling has certainly evolved, although I do not see it as a linear progression that concluded with my thesis. The research was conducted alongside the creation of the album and I continue to work with samples, therefore I am always interacting with this topic. Throughout Wahj, I work with both political and non-political samples that either have a political or non-political intention. For example, samples from my personal life, my urban surroundings, and of traditional instruments, the choice is more nuanced because it’s integrated and processed within the soundscape and ambient textures. However, for samples that are more frontal and forward, like the sampling of Amal Dunqul’s poem, “Spartacus’ Last Words” in “Madda Mudadda” the intention is more clearly deliberate and explicit. These choices are bound to spill into collective memory, as I am borrowing sounds from my surroundings and heritage. Take the sample of Lebanese singers Sabah, Wadih El Safi, and Walid Gholmieh in “Wasla”; I was drawn to their voices for reasons I can’t quite articulate. But the moment I tried fitting the sample into the track, it felt seamless. My sampling choices are meant to re-activate archive sound, and insert these historical moments into the present to let them speak again through a different context. All voice samples from the album come from televised interviews, and I chose them not only for their raw, untampered sound, but also because they carry something of the world they were recorded in. To sample them is to pull them back into light and reactivate voices forced to be erased for new audiences, while also making visible the power structures that determine whose memory is preserved and who is erased from the record. Ultimately, these sampling choices are always, in some way, in conversation with the cultural memory I carry, bringing the historical in contact with the contemporary. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items._cn_summary: Toni Geitani 的专辑《Wahj》历经五年完成，跨越十七首曲目，将电子音色、工业质感、处理化弦乐、阿拉伯声乐传统与碎裂节奏不断重新组合，每种元素始终可辨却不落入固有形态。专辑并非预设地以崩塌为主题，而是在创作环境的变化中逐渐浮现，将毁灭理解为持续共存的状态而非单一灾难。声乐在召唤与集体记忆碎片之间交替出现，如「Sawtuka」中以「即使他们束缚你、带你穿越死亡，你声音的回响将永远留存」将坚持本身转化为抵抗行为。「2092」将视角投向想象的未来，「Tuyoor」则以飞鸟意象在被压迫的天空下开辟出统治者权威之外的空间。器乐曲目「Madda Mudadda」借助仪式、重复与狂喜释放时刻承载开放性意义。整张专辑在废墟、哀悼、流亡与消失的图像之间，始终伴随光芒、回归与延续的指向，拒绝被概念本身困住。

items.body: Arshan Najafi‘s Zenosyne takes its title from John Koenig’s neologism describing the unsettling sensation that time seems to accelerate as we grow older. The album focuses on the paradox behind that sensation. As Najafi explains in the accompanying interview, the music emerged from a period in which he felt psychologically frozen while time rushed relentlessly onwards. This tension between stillness and acceleration defines the album’s two long-form electroacoustic compositions. Built from live improvisations using a piezo microphone attached to an external hard drive alongside the sonification of raw digital data, Zenosyne makes surprisingly little ceremony of its unusual sound sources. The hard drive becomes another resonant object, its vibrations feeding a semi-generative system that Najafi actively steers. Algorithmic processes introduce an element of instability, but his intervention remains central to the shape of the music. The opening “Binary Bloom” begins with almost imperceptible movement. Sustained electronic tones slowly develop interference patterns and harmonic beating, gathering momentum from within. Energy and apparent speed continue to increase without reaching a conventional climax, and the accumulated tension eventually dissipates. “Static Rotation” expands this language through a more active dialogue between pure tone and electronic noise. Its materials circulate around an unstable centre, creating perpetual motion with little sense of arrival. Najafi places considerable trust in microscopic change. Much of the musical activity remains concentrated in the lower and middle registers. Rhythm and dramatic contrast play relatively small roles, while subtle redistributions of spectral energy, minute shifts in timbre and constantly evolving resonances determine the form. Musical time is stretched sufficiently for these small changes to acquire unusual weight, sharpening our awareness of its passing. To get an idea of Arshan Najafi’s live process, here is a recording of one of his no-input mixer and computer sets, followed by an interview about the making of Zenosyne. Zenosyne takes its title from John Koenig’s neologism and yet the album doesn’t seem to represent memory nostalgically. Instead, both “Binary Bloom” and “Static Rotation” seem to suspend chronological time altogether, creating spaces in which microscopic changes become more significant than linear progression. How did the idea of Zenosyne shape your compositional thinking? Were you interested in evoking the psychological sensation of accelerated time, or in constructing an alternative temporal experience in which conventional notions of duration begin to dissolve? I chose the title Zenosyne because it perfectly captured my state of mind during the composition process and still does. I was experiencing this overwhelming feeling of staying completely still – almost a sense of uselessness or incapability – while watching every day pass by in a flash of light. The music reflects that paradox. The suspension of linear time you noticed in these pieces wasn’t necessarily a conceptual design to challenge musical duration, but rather a direct mirror of that personal, psychological standstill. It is the feeling of being frozen in place while time accelerates around you. Your previous releases, from Imaginary Crisis to Live at Daa Theater House, have consistently explored live electronics, improvisation and the instability of sound in performance. Zenosyne continues that trajectory, drawing on live recordings made with a piezo microphone placed on an external hard drive alongside the sonification of raw digital data. What attracted you to treating a storage device not simply as a technological object but as a resonant instrument? Did working with the physical vibrations of digital memory alter the way you think about the relationship between information, sound and materiality? I have to admit, the reason is a bit less poetic than treating the drive as a metaphor for digital memory! I have a habit of attaching piezo mics to anything that I basically can. Frankly, I don’t see much point in recording traditional acoustic instruments anymore. That’s one of the main points of electronic music for me: it obliterates the need for conventional instruments. It gives us the freedom to choose the most mundane surface or object as a sound source and manipulate it into an entirely new form. The hard drive was just a fascinating object to harvest raw frequencies from, which the computer then allows me to further process. Both pieces were improvised live in Max/MSP before being shaped during the mixing process in Ableton Live. Listening to the album, there is a constant negotiation between systems that appear algorithmic and gestures that feel spontaneous or instinctive. How do you understand improvisation when working with generative processes? Do you see yourself directing the system, collaborating with it, or responding to behaviours that emerge unexpectedly during performance? I definitely see myself as the director of the system. I design a semi-generative algorithmic environment that responds to incoming signals based on parameters I’ve dictated beforehand. I call it “semi-generative” because I intentionally build it to a point where it still requires my interaction to continue its work; it cannot sustain itself without being steered and not sound boring to me. I view live improvisation fundamentally as a technique of composing on the fly. Because there are physical, unpredictable elements – like the random fluctuations of the hard disk spinning in “Static Rotation” – I have to remain hyper-aware and react to sudden gestures, not to mention I often cause those sudden gestures myself because I feel it’s needed at that particular moment. It’s a constant dialogue between the rules I set and the behavior the system throws back at me. Your work moves fluidly between sound, image and text—you are not only a composer but also the author of Twenty Wrong Turns. Across these different media there seems to be a recurring interest in fragmentation, ambiguity and the ways meaning emerges from incomplete information. Does Zenosyne belong to that same broader artistic inquiry? More generally, how do writing and sound composition inform one another in your practice, and are there ideas that can only be explored through one medium rather than the other? To be completely honest, I haven’t consciously intertwined my music and my writing so far. I tend to treat them as separate practices that serve different purposes. However, the connection that I do see between these mediums is the word “composition” itself, as I fundamentally treat them the same way. That’s the whole point for me. While they usually exist on their own, I might occasionally bring them together – it really just depends on how I feel about a certain project. (Gianmarco Del Re)
items._genre: electroacoustic / experimental electronic / ambient drone / sound art
items._cn_summary: Najafi以"Zenosyne"（对时间加速的感知）为概念原点，通过压电麦克风拾取硬盘驱动器振动、并对原始数字数据进行声化处理，构建两首长篇电声作品。"Binary Bloom"从几乎不可感知的运动起步，持续电子长音在内部缓慢发展干涉图案与谐波拍频，能量持续累积却拒绝传统意义上的高潮；"Static Rotation"则在纯音与电子噪声之间建立更活跃的对话，材料围绕不稳定中心循环往复。算法过程引入不稳定性，但演奏者的实时操控仍居核心地位。作品将音乐时间充分拉伸，使频谱能量的微观重新分配、音色的细微偏移成为结构主导力量，听者的时间意识因此被锐化与重塑。

items.body: Hawgood has tied Folk Reels to the idea of a mobile archive, a repository for scattered works, old tapes and encounters. Live At Still Point 2026 introduces a welcome fissure into that archive. To preserve also means admitting loss and giving it an audible measure. A work that fully embraces the loss it suffered and transforms it into living matter Live at Still Point 2026 by Ian Hawgood   A live album promises to bear witness, a weighty claim, perhaps too weighty. It evokes the idea of an event fixed once and for all, destined to return unchanged with every listen. Live At Still Point 2026 favors a memory with sections erased, passages heard only by those present at Brimscombe Mill that afternoon. The recording preserves the core of Ian Hawgood’s performance, while the contributions of two laptops used for processing were never captured in the file. A tangible absence, then, which has become the defining character of the work itself. The released sound recognizes its own limits and reveals them with rare candor. For Hawgood, the concert marked his return to performing before an audience after seven years. That fact carries more weight than a line in a press release, since his artistic journey has always sought a human dimension in the act of listening. A British sound engineer, founder of Home Normal and custodian of Folk Reels, he has built an extensive catalog around care, collaboration, tape and field recordings. At Still Point, that principle reconnects with the risk of the moment and a freedom still capable of play. Twenty five minutes, a single movement. At first come rustling sounds, calls whose source is difficult to place, brief electrical flashes. They​ resemble tentative contacts taking the measure of the air. Then a deep mass expands, gathering everything happening around it. Figures from We Are But Dream are bent and pushed towards a different sense of duration. Hawgood uses SYNTRX, Buchla sequences, sounds gathered outdoors and computers running AudioMulch, instruments from different eras surrendering their names to a single current. The music grows unhurriedly and gathers body through accumulation. A melody seems about to declare itself, then immediately chooses a less determinate form. This hesitation gives the work its intensity. No backdrop inviting distraction, no contemplative postcard. Hawgood’s ambient music asks for attention in a low voice and makes perceptible the time sound requires to change its nature. From time to time, an impulse punctures the continuity, an oblique jolt roughens the balance. It happens, that is all. The performance retains a vulnerable quality, even a slight awkwardness, precious in an age obsessed with polish. Depth becomes almost physical :: In the central stretch, depth becomes almost physical. The volume rises, the fabric thickens, while the pressure avoids all monumental emphasis. Hawgood proceeds through successive degrees of proximity: one colour enters another, the drone slowly alters its light, the breathing becomes irregular. It takes time to realize that the initial landscape is already elsewhere. At the point of greatest rarefaction, the current loses substance and seems about to fade out. The music accepts this descent. From there emerge more clearly defined figures, a gentle pulse, circling scales that bring energy without breaking the spell. The ending gathers motion and a strange, purposeful serenity, as though the sound had found a way to continue after almost dispersing. Tim Diagram’s photograph translates this condition well. Trees seen from below, pale clouds, a second pattern of foliage superimposed upon the sky. The image holds two temporalities and allows them to interfere. The album likewise contains what happens and the imprint of what escapes. The material lost from the two computers compels a reconsideration of what a document can mean. The audience heard a broader version, traversed by elements that are now irretrievable; the album offers an autonomous trajectory, barer and perhaps more exposed. Fidelity lies in the gesture, its openness to chance and the human scale of what has been preserved. Hawgood has tied Folk Reels to the idea of a mobile archive, a repository for scattered works, old tapes and encounters. Live At Still Point 2026 introduces a welcome fissure into that archive. To preserve also means admitting loss and giving it an audible measure. The still point evoked by the title becomes a magnetic centre around which everything changes: intensity, distance, density, memory. This is where the album’s achievement lies. Its beauty arises from a restrained decision: to release what survived without consoling reconstruction and to entrust absence with an active role. At the end, an unusual feeling lingers. Has one listened to a concert, or to the memory that a concert produced inside a machine? The question matters more than any answer. Hawgood offers twenty five minutes freed from the pose of the celebratory live album and the smoothness of the ambient product. The sound breathes, falters, gathers strength and recedes. In that movement it carries with it the Still Point community, the apprehension of returning, the pleasure of experimentation and the part that no medium will ever be able to hold. A work that fully embraces the loss it suffered and transforms it into living matter. Live at Still Point 2026 is available on folk reels. items.body: Giulio Aldinucci has made an album that seems acquainted with the unnamed part of human nature, the part that surfaces in sleep or in the few seconds before news capable of changing the course of a day. Rhythm is felt through changes in pressure Materia by GIULIO ALDINUCCI   At first there is weight. A quiet, almost geological pressure that arrives before recognition, touching the body before it reaches the mind. Materia begins in that dark place. Sound has volume, temperature, even something resembling a will of its own. It advances slowly and alters the scale of things, like a sudden bank of fog moving in. Sight loses its authority and the ear becomes a larger organ. Giulio Aldinucci has made an album that seems acquainted with the unnamed part of human nature, the part that surfaces in sleep or in the few seconds before news capable of changing the course of a day. The composer, born in Siena, Tuscany, reaches this point after years devoted to landscape, memory and the voice stripped of semantic meaning. The experience developed under the name Obsil and the chapter that began with Tarsia have shaped a coherent body of work, nourished by field recordings, choral presences and electronic transformations. Borders And Ruins examined the nature of territory; Disappearing In A Mirror and Shards Of Distant Times shifted the tension towards identity and memory; Real sought a personal reality within the excess of digital mediation. Materia, Aldinucci’s fifth album for Karlrecords, condenses that history into an essential gesture: taking a tightly packed mass of sound, carving into it, paring it back and searching for what is already alive​ inside. The album was released on September 18, 2026. Here accumulation and subtraction become emotional acts. Aldinucci gathers frequencies as scattered memories might be gathered after years apart, then removes the excess and listens into the space left behind by what has disappeared. Time, too, acquires substance. It is broken into minute units and reassembled according to an order that escapes the familiar pulse. Rhythm is felt through changes in pressure, through inner tides, through the way a distant voice rises from the haze and immediately loses its face. These are slow movements filled with secret life. Their apparent stillness is alive with motion. The six pieces form a single body lasting just under 43 minutes. Density remains the active principle, capable of changing state while retaining its gravity. The depths below sustain the journey with a telluric continuity. Above them appear distorted choirs, echoes, drifting particles and sounds that preserve a human trace after language and origin have fallen away. The titles sketch a constellation of absence: “Not Here,” the shadow cast by noise, ash and distant waves, the absolute finality of “Never,” evening, then light caught in a dream. The music receives these images and preserves their indeterminacy. Each one works within the act of listening, removed from plot and close to the freedom of involuntary association. “Materia finds its human center here. The album’s grandeur springs from this dizzying proportion: an immense sound holds a tiny gesture, perhaps a mouth drawing breath, perhaps a syllable worn away by time.” ~Mirco Salvadori The voice is central. It rises like a collective memory without face or biography, suspended between comfort and alarm. At times it resembles someone calling across an immense distance; elsewhere it takes on the substance of a thought formed in the body before words. Aldinucci understands the power of vocal fragments and frees them from any narrative duty. What remains is breath, impulse, a tremor that reminds the listener of human fragility. Materia finds its human center here. The album’s grandeur springs from this dizzying proportion: an immense sound holds a tiny gesture, perhaps a mouth drawing breath, perhaps a syllable worn away by time. “Come Luce, In Sogno,” chosen as the advance single, offers a discreet way into the album. The light invoked by its title contains dust and density. It filters through opaque layers and produces figures already moving towards dissolution. Dreaming becomes a mode of knowledge. A detail can expand until it fills the entire field of perception, while an enormous event contracts into a brief vibration. This instability runs through the whole work. Time seems to lengthen; then an almost imperceptible shift alters the landscape. Sound retains warmth and a question that has yet to find words. The cover helps reveal the character of the work. A white façade multiplies concave modules, dark openings and curves that look identical only at a glance. The eye finds order, then differences, shadows, stains and minor signs of wear. It is a serial form made vulnerable by time and by the material from which it is built. Aldinucci’s music behaves in much the same way. It turns repetition into change, raises immense structures and allows irregularity to bring them alive. Each surface hints at another depth. No answer comes. The desire to look again grows stronger. The concentration of the sound demands complete attention. A moment’s distraction can break the spell, and some passages deliberately court saturation. This is an exacting choice. Materia requires time, an appropriate volume and a measure of solitude. In return it offers a rare experience, moving listening beyond taste and into consciousness. Its forms entrust their appeal to a slower force, like the memory of a place never visited. There is familiarity and a faint fear. The unknown takes on an intimate temperature. “Sound appears as something that precedes its maker and continues beyond its listener, bound to the same matter as bodies, air and thought.” ~Mirco Salvadori Throughout Aldinucci’s career, recording the world has carried the value of a living archive. A landscape could hold a story; a procession could deliver into the present voices already receding into the distance; an ordinary noise could open a passage through perception. Materia brings this practice close to an elemental dimension. Here substance comes before place and contact before narrative. Sound appears as something that precedes its maker and continues beyond its listener, bound to the same matter as bodies, air and thought. This is where its power lies. The album speaks of the human condition through feeling. The need to give chaos a shape meets the fascination of whatever resists a final form. Every cut removes part of the original mass; subtraction reveals an unforeseen outline. The music breathes between these impulses, tightens, withdraws and fills out again. At times it seems about to disclose something. Then that something changes substance and becomes pure listening. Materia is expansive, gathered into a fierce intensity and charged with physical mystery. Giulio Aldinucci reaches one of the most mature expressions of his artistic language and gives contemporary ambient music an album with moral as well as sonic weight. When the final vibration ends, silence feels altered, thicker, almost conscious. Within that silence passes an intuition that cannot quite be held: perhaps the human spirit is precisely this restless substance, seeking form while knowing that every form is temporary. For just under 43 minutes, Materia gives it a body and lets it sing. Materia is available on Karlrecords. items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — An unusual yet fully-progressive undertaking of setting literary stories to music using jazz-fusion artists.1. "The Sinking Spell" (4:40) Robert Wyatt's distinctive voice enters with some effect applied while the four musicians, Steve Swallow, Jack DeJohnette, Carla Bley, and Terje Rypdal apply their talents to constructing a loose and reactive soundtrack to Robert's rendering of this Edward Gorey story. Terje is particularly flamboyant (almost in a Steve Hackett way!) while Carla, Steve, and Jack are pretty dynamic in their own right. Perhaps Robert's best, most unique performance on the album and maybe the best collective Jazz-Rock Fusionary exposition as well. (9.125/10) 2. "The Object Lesson" (5:00) piano, bass and swelling cymbal crashes back Robert's rather flat/monotone delivery of this story. Eventually the musicians fall into a kind of groove with Jack DeJohnette's rock drumming and Terje Rypdal and Carla Bley's Canterbury organ saw-like expressions. The music is not great, not fully-formed or composed for much other than dramatic support, but it works (it's better than the story being told). (8.75/10)3 "The Insect God" (5:00) some truly top-notch Jazz-Rock Fusion is used to present another sobering and not-for-children's-ears story. The music quartet of Bley, Rypdal, Swallow, and drummer Jack DeJohnette are all on the same page of aggressive and insistent delivery while Robert and spoken-word "backing vocalists" render their fast-talking approach to dramatic story-telling. (8.75/10)4 "The Doubful Guest" (4:45) finally! some thoroughly-composed music! It's a challenging weave of off-timed hi-speed drum and keyboard music in which Steve and Terje contribute long-held, pensive notes on their respective instruments. All the while Robert delivers a near-spoken word story with a little more flair and enthusiasm than the past two. The overall weave really works--has no glaring flaws or inconsistencies. I like the way the musical performances ramp up toward the end: especially Terje's guitar shredding and Carla's breadth of synth strings chords. (9.125/10)5 "The Remembered Visit" (6:25) voice with syncopated bass and synth-strings pulses, adding piano and Mellotron "ooo"s and "aaah"s, then treated electric guitar notes and some background drumming. In the third minute the drums and bass play get more animated--still orchestral and reactive, though, more than "song" oriented. Where Robert's delivery starts out dramatic and engaged, it begins to sound a bit like rote reading in places. But then things slow down for the background vocal-supported passage in the fifth minute--which has the effect of seeming to bring Robert back into the spirit of the story. From there out he feels fully-present in his story-telling. Effective. (8.875/10)6 "The Hapless Child" (7:00) Robert Wyatt's distinctive voice and vocal/story-telling stylings are here backed by music that feels more like theater music: it's incidental and yet has a personality all its own--as if taking on the characteristics of Robert's story's characters. Nothing is flowing or timed, almost all of it feels impressionistic and reactive more than composed and prescribed. There is one theme that feels prepared: the whole-band motif that starts at 2:58 when Robert starts singing about the start of Charlotte Sophia's boarding school experience, but at 4:20 everything devolves to simple piano--just before launching into a more dynamic and drum-and-guitar-driven theme. What a horrifying Dickensian tale! Carla Bley's odd chord choices hold the whole thing down but it's Steve Swallow's obtuse bass notes and Terje Rypdal's sharp, stinging guitar notes that bring forth and amplify the Poe-like atmosphere of the story. Wow! What an experience! Definitely not your typical bed-time story! Even children's theatre would be scarred and marred for decades if they brought children in to hear this one! Still, it is a rather powerful and effective delivery mechanism. (13.25/15)Total Time:I have to admit that I was not prepared for either the album's total dedication to story telling nor it's dark and rather dismal, even desolate, Dickensian/Brothers Grimm/Edgar Allen Poe story lines. While I love the literate nature of the stories, I'm a bit disturbed by their unsettling subject matters. At the same time, I appreciate these adventurous musicians for their commitment to the expansion of that which music and Jazz-Rock Fusion can do. B/four stars; though admirable to take on such an odd and ambitious undertaking, I feel that the stories and music do not always match as well as the artists/producers may have wanted. Nor are the instrumental performances and song/soundtrack compositions as polished and coordinated as well as one might expect or desire from this stellar line-up.

items._cn_summary: 这是迈克尔·曼特勒1976年的作品，将爱德华·戈瑞的暗黑文学故事配以爵士融合音乐。核心编制包括罗伯特·怀亚特独特的念白演唱、吉他手特里耶·吕普达尔、贝斯手史蒂夫·斯沃洛、鼓手杰克·迪约翰内特以及键盘手卡拉·布莱。专辑将叙事文学与器乐融合，六首作品各自呈现不同的配器策略：有时以钢琴、贝斯与镲片构建戏剧性背景，有时以激进急促的节奏群推进叙事，有时则以精密编排的合成器弦乐与错位鼓点编织复杂织体。整体呈现出戏剧配乐与自由爵士融合的实验倾向，文学叙事与器乐反应式互动构成核心创作逻辑，独立厂牌发行保留了其艺术探索的非商业取向。

items.body: With Hor-Cheret, we welcome a new project presented as a collaboration between members of Vortex, Nam-Khar, and Delta Komplex, complemented by a few more artists. The project’s name alludes to Horus, the child of Isis and Osiris in Egyptian mythology. With an album title referring to an ancient nomadic law of hospitality, Hor-Cheret offers an intriguing metaphor and, in my view, a critical perspective on today’s world. It certainly offers food for thought, but above all, this is music to be discovered. From the very first notes, a distinct Ritual influence emerges through the percussion and the use of traditional acoustic instruments. While the percussion reinforces the album’s ritualistic character, the listener gradually discovers a dark atmosphere shaped by deep sound waves. Elements of Dark-Ambient and Industrial music are clearly present. An Ethereal female voice occasionally takes on a narrative role while simultaneously enhancing the sense of mysticism. The male voice also serves a narrative function, while some of the lyrics possess a distinctly poetic quality. This is a superbly crafted album in a genre that suffers from a lack of quality projects and inconsistent production standards. Hor-Cheret’s debut is a release to be savored and cherished. (Rating:8½). Listen to “In The Shadow Ov Power”: In The Shadow Ov Power by HOR-CHERET About Hor-Cheret Hor-Cheret is a new collaborative project pairing members of Vortex, Nam-Khar and Delta Komplex with additional contributors, presented on Dunkelheit Produktionen. Its name references Horus, the child of Isis and Osiris in Egyptian mythology. Nam-Khar is the ritual ambient project of Romanian musician Konchog Gyaltsen, active since 2009, previously paired with Vortex on “Nag-Hammadi” in 2022 and “The Sarajevo Spiral” in 2024. Delta Komplex is a German electronic band founded in 2019 around Minu-Schirin Samimi and Tufana, known for the 2022 album “Veils”. “Nanawatai”, Hor-Cheret’s debut album, was released on 7 November 2025 in a limited handnumbered digipak edition.

items.body: His curved neck bent right back to see the swan Dreading the four steps up and over to where we ran I reached the viewing point and I sit here watching and waiting But then sometimes life’s unkind Boston’s GOSSIP COLLAR makes post-punk as though somebody locked Ladytron in an abandoned theater with a deathrock band, a stack of Killing Joke records, several reels of damaged fairy-tale film, and instructions that nobody gets out until dawn. Somewhere behind the electronic throb and serrated guitar on their latest offering, the EATEN OF WORMS LP, there is also the emotional breadth of the Chameleons, a little Breeders crookedness, and that marvelous early-goth conviction on bass guitar. The band began with best friends playing and dancing in a dark Boston basement at the tail end of the pandemic, drawing together members of The Showcase Showdown, Spitzz, and Secret Hearts. They describe this incarnation as their “dark punk chapter,” which sounds about right, though “chapter” seems almost too civilized for music filled with drowning sailors, torn bodies, predatory birds, collapsing circuses, religious dread, and people standing beside freezing seas wondering precisely when existence developed such a personal vendetta. There are obvious ancestral spirits here: Xmal Deutschland, Parálisis Permanente, early Siouxsie and the Banshees, the strange congregation that gathered around the London Batcave when punk discovered it could wear theatrical makeup without surrendering its teeth. They sound less interested in reconstructing 1982 than in asking what happens when those old poisons get poured into present-day arteries. Their live pedigree adds another clue. GOSSIP COLLAR have shared stages with The March Violets, Pink Turns Blue, Rendez-Vous, Haunt Me, House of Harm, Fotocrime, and Sympathy Flowers, placing them comfortably among bands for whom darkness still needs rhythm, muscle, and enough propulsion to keep bodies moving even while the songs are busy describing spiritual ruin. Throughout the songs on EATEN OF WORMS, nature rarely provides comfort. Seas threaten to swallow people, birds wait for flesh, wolves pursue deer, plants cut skin, rain destroys, and the night contains forces that clearly have not received the memo about personal boundaries. GOSSIP COLLAR’s apocalyptic fairy tale grows out of this collision between childhood imagery and adult terror, where forests, animals, oceans, and old religious symbols have all turned slightly hostile. Edgar Froese once said, “There is no death, there is just a change of our cosmic address.” GOSSIP COLLAR sound perfectly capable of furnishing the house he moved into. Disguise My Heart opens with a saxophone-like drone, its low complaint quickly overtaken by a deep, quick-moving bassline and drums that strike with the urgent physical force of Joy Division’s Love Will Tear Us Apart. The guitars pick out a cold, melodic figure before heavier layers gather around it, giving the song a density that makes the vocal seem to travel from somewhere beyond the instruments. Witchy and windblown, the voice calls through the mix with a banshee’s sense of occasion, stretching the distance between the rhythm section’s forward charge and the solitary figure waiting beside the Northern Sea. Freezing water, aching eyes, and blood threatening to turn cold give emotional injury a bodily presence; the guitars seem to press against the skin as insistently as the memories. Even as the drums push onward, the song remains fixed on that desolate stretch of coastline. Heartbreak becomes architectural here: eventually you stop carrying it around and simply move into it. Scavengers follows with a sheet of cold guitar and an insistent bass throb, burying an unusually inviting melody several layers into the disturbance. When the arrangement briefly catches its breath, the bass leads the voice into view, exposing the sharp, declamatory cadence beneath its witchy inflections. There is an anarcho-punk edge to the delivery, a sense that these words are being hurled across a room even as the guitars make that room feel enormous. That force suits a song whose speaker lies broken, bleeding, and apparently available to whatever happens to be circling overhead. The hook keeps drawing the ear back through the commotion while memories collect like personal debris beside the body. Death may happen quickly, destruction takes its time, and the promise of resurrection supplies a final complication. Apparently even carrion birds are going to have to wait their turn. A brief arc of distortion introduces Big Top Comes Crashing Down, followed by a jagged guitar figure that rings with the blunt insistence of a tolling bell. Once the drums and bass hit, the riff acquires a crooked melodic momentum, turning its initial severity into something almost indecently catchy. Above it, the vocal echoes with a thunderous breadth, making the performance feel much larger than the cramped emotional circumstances it describes. White greasepaint goes on, the smile gets rehearsed again, and another day disappears beneath the effort of remaining presentable. That circling guitar figure becomes an apt accompaniment to the work of doing it all again tomorrow. The image of someone maintaining the same expression for ten years on Exmouth Street carries the ugly comedy of a photograph that has outlived everybody’s patience. Keep smiling hard enough and sooner or later your face becomes part of the prison. Haerisis gives the bass room to announce itself, opening with a thick, deliberate strut locked to the drumbeat. Sustained guitar tones spread above that steady march, and the clearer placement of the vocal lets its chanting insistence register more directly. The arrangement has a substantial physical weight, with dense guitar chords and more melodic lines carrying on around a groove that remains easy to follow through all the theological panic. Blood, broken bones, forbidden chalices, frozen streams, wolves, and deer crowd the lyrics, turning belief into a landscape where almost everything can injure you. The sustained tones lend those images a sense of scale, while the rhythm section keeps their violence close enough to feel. There is something particularly effective about the orderly tread beneath all this religious dread: the song advances with the certainty of a procession whose destination nobody has thought to question. On Dead Thing, a heavy wash of guitar gives way to the splash and momentum of the drums, with the opening density settling into a firm support for the melody. Another weighty riff sweeps through the arrangement, while a persistent guitar drone keeps pressure on the spaces between its movements. The vocal sounds cavernous, its thunderous resonance making each phrase seem to return from the far end of a large, inhospitable room. Those overlapping guitar textures give the song’s fascination with self-destruction considerable force. Lions are led by their manes, weapons are made, and human ingenuity eventually discovers the convenience of turning its own inventions inward. Scars become evidence and shame becomes inheritance, yet the drums maintain enough movement to make the plea for dancing feel entirely plausible. Tenderness enters through the side door wearing funeral clothes, and the rhythm section has already made room for it. Why Me? begins with eerie chimes and a low drone, suggesting an old piano being played somewhere beyond the inhabited rooms of a house. A thick bass figure gradually establishes the song’s tension, recalling the stalking movement of the Cure’s A Forest with considerably more weight behind each step. The vocal holds its heat close, sounding troubled and intimate against the spacious opening. Around the halfway point, heavier guitars enter and the arrangement settles into a cold gothic-rock groove, increasing the pressure while keeping its movements controlled. That restraint gives the lyrics’ grotesque physical imagery additional bite. Red lips, internal screaming, and organs hanging from trees turn desire into a form of captivity, while the bass continues its patient inspection. The fascination directed toward the speaker feels increasingly forensic, as though somebody has been pinned beneath a collector’s glass and asked to appreciate the compliment. The uneasy string-like tones and warbles that open Peaceful in Daylight make its title seem optimistic well before the kick drum lands. Arcs of cold guitar stretch across the entrance, then the full beat pushes the song into motion, carrying heavy riffs and a vocal whose witchy bite grows sharper against the instrumental weight. Seaweed, dense smoke, cutting thorns, broken walls, injured skin, and abandoned nests accumulate in the lyrics, filling the song with evidence that something has gone badly wrong. The arrangement gives that damaged environment a restless physical life; every forward push seems to uncover another unpleasant detail. An old-school rock guitar solo adds a flash of theatrical excess, briefly letting the instrument take over the voice’s fevered work. Daylight may make this place easier to inspect, but there is very little in the music to suggest that inspection will bring reassurance. Spelling Misery initially gives its guitar melody a clear view of the room. The figure rises and falls over a solid rhythm section, its easy memorability providing a point of reference before heavier guitars and dark vocals crowd into the arrangement. Further melodic details appear as the song progresses, with a recurring gothic-rock guitar phrase adding small complications to the surrounding force. Those returns keep the ear attached to the song even as its family portrait becomes increasingly difficult to look at. Anger lives in the blood, a father kills the fatted calf in nervous rage, and memory falters under the effort of naming what has happened. Biblical promises of shelter follow: arrows will fail, feathers will cover the vulnerable body, and fear might be held outside for another night. The returning guitar figure offers a little steadiness amid those appeals, though the heavier passages make the promised protection feel precarious. Unsafe State opens with a buzzing synthesizer pulse and cold electronic tones, briefly suggesting a turn toward synthwave before the melodic resonance of the post-punk guitars establishes its place on the record. The vocal sits more clearly in the mix, and its somber delivery makes the song’s vulnerability unusually exposed. Where other tracks enlarge their distress through dense guitars and cavernous echoes, this one allows the words to feel nearer, with the electronic repetition giving them an uneasy regularity. Eyes lose their rhythm, time becomes a dark tunnel, and the speaker digs until their nails hurt while dead souls call from somewhere nearby. The guitar melody carries that distress with a fragile clarity, giving the song an emotional directness that makes its domestic setting especially troubling. Home is supposed to provide some distance from danger; here, danger has apparently obtained a key. The closing Merchants of the Wave begins with a bassline that shifts up and down, setting a rolling motion beneath a classic post-punk guitar figure. Broader gothic-rock arcs develop around that melody, while the ghostly vocal seems suspended above the rhythm section’s steady movement. The arrangement gives the record’s returning ocean imagery a physical shape: friends venture onto dangerous seas, boats pitch, beds shake with frantic dreams, and tears become indistinguishable from salt water. The bass keeps the song moving beneath those anxious visions, its rises and falls suggesting the uncertain footing of people trying to remain upright. Prayer repeats because repetition may be the only available defense against forces too large to negotiate with. The sea that opened the album as a place of private emotional exposure becomes a shared source of fear here, carrying the possibility that somebody loved might disappear beyond reach. GOSSIP COLLAR keeps returning to bodies under pressure: freezing, bleeding, scratched, exposed, dissected, exhausted, threatened with consumption or drowning. Yet these bodies persist. They dance. They pray. They disguise themselves. They paint their faces. They get abandoned to scavengers and announce plans to rise anyway. Musically, that stubbornness comes through in the combination of deathrock abrasion and electronic precision. Imagine Ladytron discovering a box of Killing Joke singles beneath the floorboards, then recruiting the Chameleons to widen the horizon while somebody from the Breeders quietly rearranges the furniture. Beneath all the gothic architecture runs punk’s ancient belief that anxiety becomes considerably more useful once somebody gives it a bassline. That may be why GOSSIP COLLAR’s particular apocalypse remains so inviting. Civilization has collapsed, the circus tent is falling, the sea wants your body, God may or may not be answering correspondence, and several animals appear to have questionable intentions. Fine. There is still a song playing downstairs. Might as well dance before the scavengers get here. Listen to EATEN OF WORMS below and order the album, out now via Bat-Cave Productions, here. items._cn_summary: 波士顿乐队GOSSIP COLLAR在专辑《Eaten of Worms》中以阴郁的后朋克框架为基底，融合了deathrock的戏剧张力与冷波低音线条。评论将其声音比作将Ladytron锁入废弃剧院与deathrock乐队共处一室的产物，引用了Xmal Deutschland、Siouxsie and the Banshees等早期哥特先驱的精神血脉。乐队将自然意象——海洋、掠食鸟类、狼群、雨夜——转化为童年童话与成人恐惧之间的碰撞场域，宗教符号与动物寓言共同构成启示录式的叙事。歌词涉及溺水者、撕裂的躯体、崩塌的马戏团，呈现出一种带有古老毒性的当代哥特美学，而非简单复刻1982年的声响。评论通过对单曲《Disguise My Heart》的逐曲分析，展示了乐队如何利用无人机般的低频嗡鸣、Joy Division式的鼓击紧迫感以及层层叠加的吉他密度来构建情绪张力，强调黑暗氛围仍需节拍与推进力来支撑肢体律动。

items.body: The German duo Grimoire De Occulte has been active for several years now and has released the majority of its work, particularly in recent years. Inspired by Bernd Hermanns, aka ‘Baal’ (owner of Dunkelheit Produktionen and also active in several other projects), and ‘Philosoph’, they originally released this album in 2025, with the CD version following this year. The title word ‘Ajna’ undoubtedly refers to the Sanskrit word usually translated as ‘perceiving’, ‘knowing’, or ‘insight’. It also represents the sixth chakra, which is associated with the so-called third eye. This aligns perfectly with the approach of this project, which has always been closely linked to ritual and mysticism. We are presented with an elaborate and unique track lasting nearly 40 minutes. “Ajna: Transmissions” invites the listener to immerse themselves in an esoteric world in which the ‘other side’ plays a prominent role. This naturally provides inspiration for a dark composition, with the duo presenting us with a persistent, ominous wave of sound. At first glance, it may seem somewhat monotonous, yet the composition is enriched with humming sound effects and additional sounds, including all kinds of crackling field recordings. The whole piece is also punctuated by a scream, which adds extra power to the dark ritual. As far as I’m concerned, a few additional tracks could have been included here, but this extended “Ajna: Transmissions” remains a pleasant listen nonetheless. (Rating:7½). Listen to “Anja: Transmissions”: Ajna: Transmissions by Grimoire De Occulte About Grimoire De Occulte Grimoire De Occulte is a German duo formed by Bernd Hermanns, also known as “Baal” and the owner of Dunkelheit Produktionen, together with “Philosoph”. The project’s discography traces back to the 2011 cassette EP “Funeral Lands” on Dunkelheit Produktionen, followed by the self-released 2012 rehearsal tape “Rehearsal November 2012″ and the 2017 split 7” “Dschinn… / Atardecer De Mayo” with Mirthless, also on Dunkelheit Produktionen. Further releases include “Ritual Before Thy Fullmoon (Rehearsal)” (2017) and the self-released cassette “Calling The Ancient Fears” (2021), before the duo returned to Dunkelheit Produktionen for the CD album “Sinister Rituals” (2023) and now “Ajna: Transmissions”, issued digitally in 2025 and on CD in 2026.
items._cn_summary: 德国二人组Grimoire De Occulte发行专辑《Ajna: Transmissions》，标题取自梵语，象征第三眼脉轮，与项目一贯的神秘仪式主题高度契合。整张专辑仅由一首近四十分钟的单一长篇作品构成，以持续延展的低沉嗡鸣音墙为核心，辅以人声哼鸣、嘶叫以及大量来自田野录音的噼啪声响，营造出幽暗而凝滞的仪式氛围。整体编曲刻意维持在单调的频率域内推进，使听者沉入一种被动的冥想状态。该作品最初以数字形式发行，后由独立厂牌Dunkelheit Produktionen推出CD版本。受限于单轨极简结构，乐评认为若能增加曲目层次会使体验更加丰富，但仍肯定其作为氛围型仪式音乐的可听性。整体定位明确趋向小众实验场景，融合暗潮、田野录音与冥想音乐元素。

items.body: Mental wormholes in the night Strange ideas give a familiar fright Some phantom power pulling you back And onto a completely different track Jack Duckworth has spent years making Soft Riot records that seem to know exactly how ridiculous modern life is, then politely invite the machines responsible over for dinner. On his latest LP, Crux, out now through Possession Records and Minimalkombinat, that dinner appears to have taken a turn. Somebody has started transmitting instructions through the walls, and Duckworth is sitting there with a synthesizer trying to determine whether the voice belongs to inspiration, paranoia, technology, or some unseen bastard who has been rewriting his lines while he sleeps. Ghostwriter sets the idea in motion with a Motorik beat, clipped electronics, and Duckworth’s sprechstimme delivered with the disciplinary authority of someone reading factory regulations during an evacuation. There is something of Nitzer Ebb and Suicide in the chant, Fad Gadget in the nervous intelligence, and Skinny Puppy in the sense that electronic equipment might eventually develop opinions about its owner. Elsewhere, the stylish severity of Japan, Bill Nelson’s eccentric futurism, Simple Minds before stadiums swallowed them, and late-period Wire all seem to inhabit the same crooked apartment building. Prince lurks somewhere downstairs, idly wondering why everybody is dressed so seriously. The song concerns creation becoming possession. Ideas appear without explanation, strange mental tunnels open after dark, and ordinary thought gets interrupted by transmissions whose sender remains unknown. Duckworth turns writer’s intuition into supernatural interference: inspiration as somebody else grabbing the steering wheel. His video makes that concept gloriously physical. Forget the standard musician-stares-meaningfully-at-camera routine. Duckworth does that, but becomes part of a universe of printed graphics, hand animation, projected textures, surreal juxtapositions, and visual jokes that recall Dada photomontage, Saul Bass title sequences, and the wonderfully deranged graphic vocabulary of 80s television. Everything looks cut, pasted, shoved sideways, photographed again, and allowed to misbehave. All animations were made physically, with printed graphics manipulated by hand, while projector imagery was filmed again to produce the backgrounds and textures. Duckworth handled the graphics and editing, with assistance from Leyre Mann Vadillo. That analogue process becomes part of the argument: “This allowed me not only to get off the computer for most of the creation of this video, but also opened up the doors really wide for collaboration with other people in a far more intuitive and inclusive way,” says Duckworth. “This allowed the usage of computer software to be basic and minimal, mainly keying out backgrounds, levels, colourising and layering of the animated footage. As I feel the world of what I recognize as an underground music scene and community keeps getting more absorbed into the world of statistics, data and marketing that is more in line with late-stage capitalism, it was important for me to focus on things in the real world like working with other people, meeting new ones, connecting with people, traveling and performing live. The digital world today is planned, created, and orchestrated by the corporations that build it — a far cry from the more utopian possibilities the internet held when I first got acquainted with it in the 90s. The physical world, however, is something that we still don’t know the purpose of yet, despite thousands of years of humans trying to speculate why it exists. Ultimately, the digital world we’ve created can’t exist without the physical world it sits in — not the other way around.” Watch the video for Ghostwriter below: With Ghostwriter Jack Duckworth has made a song about invisible influence while creating its visual counterpart with scissors, paper, projectors, hands, and other people. In an era increasingly obsessed with converting creativity into metrics, his forthcoming album Crux finds Soft Riot asking a useful question: when an idea suddenly appears inside your head, who exactly handed it to you? Listen to Ghostwriter below and order Crux here. items.body: Pendulum is a singular piano trio featuring French pianist Benoît Delbecq with Danish double bass player Jonas Westergaard and drummer Peter Bruun (both Westergaard and Bruun have collaborated before with fellow Danish pianist Søren Kjærgaard). Bruun initiated this trio in 2024 as part of his ambitious research project exploring new approaches to musical time (Multitemporal movement and embodiment through Rhythmic Design at The Danish National Academy of Music). The Pendulum trio investigates all aspects of this classic format, including the most basic sensibilities of space and time, avoiding rigid structures, allowing instead for balance, elegance and fluidity. It challenges us to listen to its music as resonant arcs or shared fields of presence rather than defined by linear time, and explores new ways to transform free improvisation gravity into groove. Delbeq suggested that the trio will play with the presence of physical pendulums on stage, symbolizing the elasticity of time and giving a sense of pulse. These oscillating bodies guide the subtle, cyclical shifts in the music, which, paradoxically, feels familiar: music that sways and breathes, while finding rhythm in the inevitability of motion. The trio releases its eight-volume EP series, Arcs , nearly three hours of music, in a monthly release cycle that began in May and will conclude in December 2026. These Arcs offer Pendulum’s idiosyncratic, enigmatic, lyrical universe, in which metric relations, shifting balances, and elastic phrasing are woven together in a kaleidoscopic manner. Each volume swings on its own terms, with no intention to offer a linear narrative, and uses distinct compositional fragments, notated and graphic scores. But the whole project accumulates into an open body of work that allows us to feel how time bends, breathes, and searches for an elusive balance. The Pendulum trio invites listeners to form their own path through the eight volumes and discover different insights and relations in their own time. Arc No. 1 Pendulum describes this volume: “Time leans before it moves. Motion unfolds patiently, stretching and rebounding with quiet elasticity. What propels the arc is not force but attentiveness, which allows duration to bend and return without breaking. Each swing carries clarity and restraint, revealing time as something more shaped than measured”. The trio suggests sparse, deep listening, labyrinthine architectures with patient and subtle, cyclical-rhythmic shifts, best captured in the aptly titled, 17-minute minimalist “Exercice Elastique”, that patiently gravitates into a most delicate, vulnerable, quite irreverent groove. Arc No. 2 “Afterwards appears before it is recognized. Movement writes itself into space, leaving subtle traces that guide listening rather than direction. Rhythms form paths, both adaptable and responsive, where perception stretches between memory and anticipation. The arc remains fluid, shaped by change rather than arrival”. Pendulum sketches an almost abstract, empty map, from which it begins to imagine possible contours and paths, and how to find its inner, spatial logic, and its subtle rhythmic shifts, finally realized on “Plasticity”. Arc No. 3 “Movement turns inward. Each gesture is weighted, deliberate, and reduced to necessity. Time thickens as motion slows, inviting attention to settle inside the smallest shifts. The arc transforms discreetly, as intensity is held beneath restraint. Balance is discovered through presence, not display”. The 31-minute “Buto” corresponds with the hyper-slow and hyper-controlled motion of the Japanese avant-dance theatre, Butō (舞踏), that resists and fixated conception of time. Pendulum’s fragile balance was realized through an austere, cryptic, and often almost silent presence that keeps triggering our imagination, and not by technical display or mastery. Arc No. 4 “Wooden time moves with grain and resistance. Motion creaks, sways, and negotiates its own structure. Oscillation becomes tactile, shaped by friction and patience. The arc holds multiple possibilities at once, allowing form and freedom to coexist without resolution. The rings of time are both counted and counting”. The trio focuses on its essence, the ever-negotiated arcs that blur the distinction between form and freedom, and question our conception of linear time, turning it into a spiritual riddle, a kōan. Arc No. 5 “A phase shifts nearly unnoticed. Motion lightens, stepping carefully through softened contours. Layers thin and overlap, revealing phrasing where gestures begin and fade. The arc listens closely to its own balance, finding meaning in nuance rather than emphasis. The push and pull are their own reason for being”. Pendulum refines its fragile, nuanced equilibrium with melodic threads that patiently, hesitantly flirt with familiar, playful, and resonant piano trio dynamics. Arc No. 6 (to be released on October 10) “Momenta accumulate through return. Motion becomes practiced, framed by shared gravity and memory. Energy circulates without urgency, shaped by repetition and transformation. The past is present and future at once”. A further, urgent, cyclical rhythmic refinement is offered, faithfully captured in the short pieces “Arc” and “Dance”, shaped by nuanced repetitions and transformations. Arc No. 7 (to be released on November 9) “Time folds into itself. Multiple cycles coexist, asymmetrical yet connected. Movement breathes across layered durations, allowing contradiction to remain unresolved. The arc sustains density without weight, continuity without uniformity. Listening is wide enough to hold all the all of it”. Pendulum’s music plays a touch-and-go game in its own fragmented musical continuum, sustaining density without weight, continuity without uniformity, but with more structural focus. Arc No. 8 (to be released on December 9) “Strange tools reveal their logic through use. Motion disperses, leaving resonance rather than momentum. What remains feels everywhere at once, absorbed into space and attention. The arc settles without closing, as stillness carries the last trace of movement forward. It is the beginning of the end and the end of the beginning”. The concluding volume is not an end to this fascinating journey but a sort of beginning. The Pendulum trio already inhabited its own elastic conception of time, as the devoted listeners to this journey, and has established its idiosyncratic language. But Pendulum’s music tells us something deeper about life and the inevitable changes we experience throughout life. This trio asks us to adapt our time sensibility to its subtle transformations, fully embrace and be deeply attuned to our own ubiquitous cyclical and oscillating arcs, as we move forward, attempting to maintain an elusive balance. <a href="https://ilkmusiccph.bandcamp.com/album/opening-arcs-arc-no-1">Opening Arcs: Arc No. 1 by Pendulum (Benoit Delbecq, Jonas Westergaard, Peter Bruun)</a > <a href="https://ilkmusiccph.bandcamp.com/album/opening-arcs-arc-no-2">Opening Arcs: Arc no. 2 by Pendulum (Benoit Delbecq, Jonas Westergaard, Peter Bruun)</a > <a href="https://ilkmusiccph.bandcamp.com/album/pendulum-opening-arcs-arc-no-3">Pendulum – Opening Arcs: Arc no. 3 by Pendulum (Benoît Delbecq, Jonas Westergaard, Peter Bruun)</a > <a href="https://ilkmusiccph.bandcamp.com/album/pendulum-opening-arcs-arc-no-4">Pendulum – Opening Arcs: Arc no. 4 by Pendulum (Benoît Delbecq, Jonas Westergaard, Peter Bruun)</a > <a href="https://ilkmusiccph.bandcamp.com/album/opening-arcs-arc-no-5">Opening Arcs: Arc no. 5 by ILK</a > Email This BlogThis! items.album: Amsterdam CS
items.excerpt: Anyone who’s spent time in large train stations late at night or early in the morning, before the commuter rush and the busy timetables begin, will have noticed that they are quite unique sonic environments. items.body: Anyone who’s spent time in large train stations late at night or early in the morning, before the commuter rush and the busy timetables begin, will have noticed that they are quite unique sonic environments. Vast and cavernous, open at both ends, with a proliferation of hard surfaces, and heavy machinery coming and going, central stations play host to a range of interesting acoustic phenomena: resonating eddies of wind, reverberant chugging of diesel and electric engines, and echoing clatters and clamours of all sorts. Amsterdam’s central station is a prime example of such an environment, and Cinema Perdu’s latest album is both named after and created in response to it. I’m not sure how many of the sounds on the album were derived from recordings made in the station, but I wouldn’t be surprised if it was 100%. For all I know, even the melancholic string-like chords and pitched tones used here and there could have been created through some sort of filtering of recorded sound; at any rate, they sound natural, part of the whole, rather than like add-ons. The liner notes state that the intention was not to accurately document or recreate the sounds of the station as they are heard directly, and apart from a few vague snatches of tannoy announcements, obvious sonic signifiers are avoided. Yet the impression created is very much one of a large train station: the hissing and ringing, the rumble and clatter, the quiet screeches, the billowing wind, and the general hubbub all seem instantly familiar. Often this seems to have as much to do with how the sounds change as much as their qualities at any one moment. The way the quiet ambient gleams and glimmers of the opening track breathe slowly in an out, as if we were listening to the respiration of the station, is but one example of this. Or perhaps that sense of familiarity stems from the music’s ability to evoke not only the sounds of a large central train station, but also the unique state of consciousness provoked by being in one. Regular visitors to such stations will know what I mean. There’s that sense of self-effacement, of merging with the environment; the intimate yet fleeting connections with hundreds of strangers; the endless waiting. On the album’s final track, rumble, ring, and clatter slowly build, before being overtaken by soft distortion. Hiss, clamour, and the billowing of wind create a slow-moving chaos. A glimmering chord slowly blossoms and sweeps the chaos away, like the rolling to a halt of the train that will take you home. Central train stations leave unique and indelible marks on the psyche, and “Amsterdam CS” traces those marks with skill and careful attentiveness. items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

items.excerpt:

items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. The title track from the 2023 U.S. of Alchemy recording Under an Endless Sky by Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy Further reading Cris Derksen - The Visit (Review) Tiny Sun - Vanishment (Review) Maria Ka - Di Mashin (Review) Further listening You will find a number of Dorothy Moskowitz's works on Race The Sky , most recently on Podgrammes #022 and #019.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由Dorothy Moskowitz与意大利作曲家Paladino及诗人Ferrari合作，十一首曲目挑战了听众对西方和声进行的固有认知。音乐以钢琴为核心，叠加弦乐、木管、合成器音色层，在相位偏移中制造去方向感的聆听体验，类似于Steve Reich与Philip Glass的极简重复逻辑。歌词延续六十年代抗议歌曲传统，触及当代政治议题如白人至上与威权主义，同时对死亡与宇宙位置进行哲学冥想。Moskowitz的演唱不依赖传统旋律走向，而是让每个词获得独立的重量，钢琴在其中充当第二声部与希腊式评论者的角色。整体在政治自觉与声音实验之间寻找平衡，呈现了一种跨越时代回声的当代作曲实践。
