items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. items._cn_summary: Tako Toki 的第二张专辑延续了他们独特的创作路径：用废弃物品和杂料手工制作乐器——包括低音号、克拉里努特、迪吉里莫、厨房号等——然后用这些自制乐器演奏融合多种世界音乐风格的原创作品。评论特别强调这些自制乐器的音准准确性，以及它们在高质量录音下呈现的丰富声音质感。专辑曲目涵盖广泛：克莱兹默风格的欢快旋律、昆比亚风格的西班牙语合唱与拉丁打击乐、非洲节拍曲目中的木鱼和沙锤组合、桑巴与中东风格的主题。评论指出乐手在即兴段落中展现出令人印象深刻的演奏技巧，旋律线条常以爵士化的切分方式对抗节拍。整体而言，这张专辑体现了用废旧材料制作乐器的实验精神，同时以真诚的态度呈现世界音乐的多样性。

items.body: When the final sound fades, the small white emblem at the bottom of the cover comes to mind. A wave reduced to calligraphy, discreet while the blue occupies everything. Wind Paths works in much the same way: it passes through the listener, leaves behind a faint vibration and entrusts the air with carrying it away. A form capable of appearing and dissolving within a few minutes Wind Paths by Philippe Deschamps   The cover already offers a statement of intent. A shifting blue, crossed by pale brushstrokes, occupies the entire field, leaving a small white mark near the lower edge. It could be water observed at close range, air made visible, a photograph taken in motion during a crossing. The image refuses to settle. Wind Paths follows the same impulse, entrusting its identity to whatever passes, bends and changes density. Philippe Deschamps gathers wind, waves and rain into music that is brief and lucid, animated by a calm that retains its sense of movement. Four pieces and just over ten minutes form a single current. The compact running time keeps every element clear of decorative contemplation. The chords move slowly, changing color by small degrees; the guitar disperses its outlines; the synthesizers hold open an even light, gently varied from within. The field recordings enter the wider fabric discreetly. Sea and rain shed their role as illustrative background and become pressure, an irregular pulse, a measure beyond human intention. The record listens to the landscape as it transforms it. The new gesture lies in the voice. Deschamps trained as a Baroque countertenor and draws on that experience here, freeing it from text. The vocal tones stretch, overlap and take on the quality of warm currents. No phrase reaches for​ meaning. The body emerges through breath, then merges with guitar and recorded air. This fusion forms the emotional centre of the EP. It offers a fragile presence. The listener recognises a human figure and immediately watches it dissolve into the broader movement. It is a simple decision on paper, decisive in its effect. Deschamps’ path has been leading towards this synthesis for some time. Introduced to the piano as a child, later a singer, bassist and guitarist in rock and post rock groups, then trained in film sound at La Fémis, the French composer has developed an ambient body of work since 2022, nourished by natural phenomena and mental images. “Blue Baths,” “Forest of my Nights,” “The Silence of Pallas,” “Remember the Clouds,” “Endless Vanishing Lines,” and “Entering the Ocean” mark the stages of a coherent inquiry. Ocean, sky, darkness and distance provide a different organizing principle each time. Wind Paths distils that inquiry even further. The voice enters the frame and alters the relationship between landscape and memory. Intensity develops through accumulation and minute alteration :: His experience in cinema emerges through the precision of each entrance and fade. Deschamps understands the weight of a sound placed an instant earlier or later, and knows how to let a detail acquire prominence without demanding it. Here, that sensitivity produces a fluid montage. Forms follow one another through affinity, carried by a slow pulse that resembles breathing and, at times, the movement of the tide. There are no spectacular peaks, refrains or turns designed to reclaim the listener’s attention. Intensity develops through accumulation and minute alteration. At certain points, a low line supports the entire field; elsewhere, the texture grows lighter and the voice seems to arrive from an immeasurable distance. Few materials, carefully chosen. The record’s ambient purity grows from this economy. Its sound world possesses body and depth, and maintains an almost tactile transparency. Silence appears within the gaps and along the fading edges of notes. Even the fuller passages leave an open area where the wind around the listener, distant traffic or movement elsewhere in the house can still be heard. The music welcomes such intrusions. Its open character encourages a porous relationship with the present. Wind Paths can drift at low volume and preserve its identity; under closer listening, it reveals subtle changes, harmonies slipping sideways and voices layered with restraint. Such control brings its own risk. At times, the music’s gentleness brushes against a beauty held too safely, polished until friction and surprise have almost disappeared. Its brevity sharpens the issue: certain openings withdraw just as they acquire an unexpected inflection. The ending arrives early and leaves a desire for one further stretch, perhaps a little less serene. This limitation also clarifies the nature of the project. Wind Paths chooses a form capable of appearing and dissolving within a few minutes. It asks for attention without insisting upon it. The title speaks of invisible paths, and the music realizes that idea with remarkable coherence. Each element follows its own direction, guided by shared currents. The voice rises, the guitar fades, the harmonies change their angle. Deschamps has created one of his most lucid works, bringing together his vocal training, cinematic sensibility and ambient practice within a form that feels accessible, intimate and precise. When the final sound fades, the small white emblem at the bottom of the cover comes to mind. A wave reduced to calligraphy, discreet while the blue occupies everything. Wind Paths works in much the same way: it passes through the listener, leaves behind a faint vibration and entrusts the air with carrying it away. Wind Paths is available on Silent Sonic. [Bandcamp] Wind Paths by Philippe DeschampsThe post Philippe Deschamps :: Wind Paths (Silent Sonic) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.
items._cn_summary: Philippe Deschamps的EP《Wind Paths》仅由四首作品组成，总时长约十分钟出头，呈现出简洁而克制的氛围结构。专辑将风、海浪与雨声等田野录音纳入音乐织体，使其超越装饰性背景功能，转化为具有压力感的不规则脉动。Deschamps拥有巴洛克假声男高音训练背景，在作品中首次将人声从文本中解放出来，音调延展并相互交叠，与吉他和环境声融合，形成专辑的情感核心。合成器维持均匀的微变光场，吉他轮廓逐渐消散，和弦缓慢移动并通过微小幅度转换色调。短小篇幅使每一元素保持清晰，避免了氛围音乐常见的冗余沉思。这张作品延续了他自2022年以来以自然现象为灵感的创作脉络，将景观聆听转化为记忆与声音的融合实践。

items.body: Kim Cascone’s book Post-Digital Music gives sound artists the conceptual thought tools that help open up connective valves between the unconscious and conscious minds, stimulating the growth of imagination. This collection of essays is also essential reading for the continued critical discourse around issues of electronic music production and reception. Beyond knobs, plugins, and technique Some books about music making take a very materialist approach. They look at sound as a purely physical phenomenon. They look at art making as just a matter of sliding the right dials and turning the right knobs (and they love to turn knobs). They ignore the subtle side of being a musician, the synchronistic clues that align to tell an artist they are on the right path of creation, the inner knowing of when to start on a certain project, when to halt on another one, and when it might be good to revive a work left behind. There are enough books that focus on the hardware and software of music making, even as they ignore the realware of imagination. Without imagination such tools mean little or nothing. Kim Cascone’s book Post-Digital Music gives sound artists the conceptual thought tools that help open up connective valves between the unconscious and conscious minds, stimulating the growth of imagination. This collection of essays is also essential reading for the continued critical discourse around issues of electronic music production and reception. Electronic music isn’t about having a stylish se​t of tools, a modular set up that looks good on social media, or a digital studio with all the latest plugins. The tools won’t accomplish much without a musician who has grown what Goethe called “new organs of perception.” This is a phrase Cascone uses throughout his writing as a way to convey the necessity of training intuitive skills, skills at noticing the subtle, skills that can help an individual create pieces resonate with the interior life of their prospective audience, rather than just regurgitate shiny audio baubles whose sounds never reach beneath the surface.None of this is to discount the training and skill set needed to develop as a musician, songwriter or composer on the material level, but it has been shown again and again that people without the traditional pedigree of talent and virtuosity can make compelling music, while the works of virtuoso’s can be lifeless and boring. Technical chops are only half the battle. If it was all about technique, Hollywood movies would be a lot better than they are and so-called B-Films from the past would suck, but I’ve found the opposite to be true. A mind and spirit keyed in to the imaginative side of the world allows an artist in any medium to tune their own subtle senses to act as antennae for incoming seeds and ideas. Once transmuted those seeds can then be recast into the field of cultural life. The eighteen essays collected in Post-Digital Music act as a corrective to the material focus prevalent in so much of electronic music discourse over the past several decades. The essays themselves span the years 1999 to 2026 and show the evolution of Cascone’s mature thought. Many of these pieces have been around in various publications and posted online, and I had read a good chunk of them over the years before this slim volume arrived. It’s nice to have them collected all in one place, and the book can easily be tucked into a laptop bag or backpack to peruse between setting up for different gigs, recording sessions or any other time when an injection of deep thought or intellectual stimulation is required. Issues that Cascone brings up in the first short essay, “Residualism,” crop up throughout the work and are looked at from different angles all the way to the last essay “0’00” and Vertical Time.” And while they are organized sequentially in the order they were written, I have found that there are about three main topics, along with various interrelated subfields, that the essays flock and organize themselves around. The first of these topics, and a major overarching theme of his work in general is one many people are afraid to look at: failure. Cascone looks at “The Aesthetics of Failure,” ruminates on “Modulating the Boundaries of Failure” and pokes around into the possibility of failure as a window from which the future leaks out in “Errormancy: Glitch as Divination.” After a few decades of thinking about failure, and working with it in artistic computer music, he still hadn’t extracted or unpacked all that could be gleaned from its study. He included an interview titled “The Failure of Failure,” which goes beyond the notion of working with software at the edges of their prescribed ability, and takes a critical look at the failure of experimental music and art to glitch out the larger system of society. Perhaps the failure of these genres and subgenres within electronic music to change things in larger society also relates to the continued problems around performing electronic music. His essay “Laptop Music” traces the issues around live electronic music performance, specifically with computers, and it remains just as pertinent as it was when it was written in 2004. He quickly delineates the history of different kinds of music performance in the west, showing how the placing of electronic musicians on stages, and the audience in seats, as in your typical theater situation, upsets our notions of what a music performance is and should be. By way of example, I had the opportunity to see William Basinski earlier this year, and he played in a theater. He was on the stage with a tape loop, a laptop and a mixing board. I was very happy to hear this music done live, and I sat with my eyes closed for most of the show as the sounds washed over me at volumes levels I would never breach at home. When I didn’t have my eyes closed, I mostly paid attention to his video projections. His adjustments of the mixing board, computer, and loop were all very understated, and the video was in many respects its own kind of visual drone. Yet even as a fan of him, and even as someone who has played electronic music live myself with laptops and other knobby gear, the expectation around of musical performance as a kind of visual spectacle of virtuosity remain in place. As Cascone put it, “The laptop musician is conceived as a medium conducting a séance, whose tricks of table knocks, wall rapping and spectral voices broadcast from nowhere are orchestrated to feign the effect of authenticity where none really exists. Thus the cultural artifact produced by the laptop musician is deemed a counterfeit, leaving the audience unable to determine a use-value.” There still has not been much a “recuperation of codes that move away from the use of spectacle, that establish aura, and show the audience how to differentiate ‘representation by the machine’ from ‘repetition of the machine.’” Many in the audience relied on the aura of expectation created by Basinski’s albums in the live setting, or on his comedic pre and post show banter as a way to come away from the evening feeling satisfied. “The laptop musician is conceived as a medium conducting a séance, whose tricks of table knocks, wall rapping and spectral voices broadcast from nowhere are orchestrated to feign the effect of authenticity where none really exists. Thus the cultural artifact produced by the laptop musician is deemed a counterfeit, leaving the audience unable to determine a use-value.” ~Kim Cascone The other early essays remain just as relevant. The issues Cascone raised, now decades ago, are still with us. Sometimes there has been a bit of mutation along the fringes of the field, but where things have remained static, the major points are still at play. It must be remembered that electronic music is still very young as an art. The post-digital is even younger with its general focus on computer music. Perhaps a definition of just what Cascone means by Post-Digital is in order. In “Residualism” he talks about how Post-Digital music making is about the “deconstruction of audio by manipulating the prima materia itself” and how this has led to the recognition of the aesthetic value of sonic artifacts that were previously considered to be in the background. The art becomes a matter of subtracting information until only residues are left behind. While this simplifies the theoretical basis Cascone lays out, this approach and its aesthetic ramifications can be considered another core theme of the book. Because those artifacts had often been generated by pushing technology and software to the breaking point, is one of the reasons behind his intense focus failure, and how it can be a gateway into new forms of aesthetics. Another theme that emerges is a trinity around music, metaphysics and imagination. There is spiritual substance in the book, and in the works created by artists who are tuned in to the subtle fields. Essays in this grouping of include “Subtle Listening,” a text based on the workshops Cascone used to give. (These differ in form and substance from Pauline Oliveros’ work with Deep Listening, though I see the two as complimentary.) He also explores the metaphysical side in pieces such as “The Avantgarde as Aeromancy” and “The Transcenditial Imagination.” Other pieces such as “Organs of Subtle Perception” and “Imagination, Idea, Will, Manifestation” get to some of the core precepts around his percepts. His essay on aeromancy written in 2013 reflects on the artists relationship to time. Over on the blog at the Silent Records Bandcamp page, Cascone continues to write about time, about the hyper-present and how the effects of the simulacra and our immersion in online worlds pushes us into a vertical experience of time. He distinguishes this sense of verticality, of being removed from the clock-a-day world of linear horizontal time, from the kind of natural verticality we experience in moments of creative flow and time spent outside in nature.For the artist working on the horizons, at the boundaries, these distinctions are important for the work of tuning into the subtle senses and fishing for big ideas. In the essay he writes, “The past has become embedded in the future, reducing what we experience as ‘the present’ or ‘now’ -as simulacra, a plastic bauble bouncing upon the infinitesimal fulcrum where two streams intersect. One beckons from the past, the other seduces from the future. The plastic bauble of ‘now’ is all that exists today. All of time is trapped inside of it, containing a chimeric environment constructed from a trick of light, a sleight of hand, a conflation of nostalgic past with a tantalizing future.” And he continues with this salient advice: “For a real avant-garde to exist -again- we need to reestablish a ‘long-view’ perspective, recover from our collective amnesia, and locate ourselves in the larger historical landscape. By moving outside the manufactured environment and allowing the stream of time full passage through our psyches, we can return to an intuitive process of artistic divination.” “Like the artist, the audience also needs to be able to open the valve to the unconscious. Digital media in its current incarnation works as a firehose blasting the senses. Overstimulation is part of the issue. To tune in, sometimes the first step isn’t turning on, but turning off.” ~Justin Patrick Moore Now we are even more in the blurspace of the simulacra than we were in 2013. For those of us who wish to see such a return of the avant-garde as Cascone does we need to take regular time for reflection. If one of the tasks of the artist is to give reflection back, gestation periods are necessary, as is frequent time spent outside the outer focused hyper-present world, and inside the inner focused world of imagination. What bubbles inside the cauldron of a new avant-garde may take time to brew. In the world of outer of immediate action where each new piece and release vies for attention with the rest, the long term view tends to get shunted off and replaced by short term commodification, i.e. the market forces that cultivate the hyper-present simulacra for their own harvest. The larger gains that come from time spent swimming in the reflecting pool of imagination are not as apparent, not as immediate, but the long term effects could be much larger than those produced by the shiny baubles of momentary attention. For every force there is a field, and for the final grouping of general ideas I see in this book is the cluster around these words: aura, grain, and field. Field recordings have been at the heart of many approaches to electronic music for quite some time starting with the academic part of the tradition. Following the explosion of electronica, ambient, and then the plethora of interconnected subgenres, many electronicists began employing field recordings as a way to lend their pieces an organic integrity they sometimes lacked when based purely on digital sources. Ideas around the use of field recordings, and what a field actually is, all get explored at a deep theoretical level that is often missing elsewhere in the discourse. Along the way we get to learn about Cybernetics and Systems Theory (always fun and always essential) as well as flocks and the swarming behavior of genres, and how they form. All of these subjects tend to get woven into each other, one area emphasized here, another there. Reading them together, it is hard not to feel the desire to get creative. The intellectual stimulation gives me the desire to put more critical imagination into the work of making electronic music and the conversations around the field. Perhaps the greatest advice to the aspiring artist included in the book is to “lessen ones dependence on digital tools” and his admonition, via Werner Herzog, to “Read, read, read…” he suggests that composers be “voracious readers and keep a physical notebook of ideas and projects. By relying less on digital tools you will gain a valuable context for your work.” That in itself is very much another kind of Post-Digital framework. As the book began with focusing perceptions on the boundaries and edges in “Residualism,, so it ends with a piece focusing on one of the great Zen koans John Cage left behind in the form of a musical composition. It is a seldom talked about piece of music that he wrote, 0”00”. It is a work that has no duration, and in many ways, it only exists in the mind. By going back to this ground zero, we are left in a kind of recursive mobius strip, zeroing back in on zero itself. Cascone again cautions against getting too caught up in the speed race of digital acceleration. He also reminds us that the collective suite of digital tools that now exist to make things by command, i.e., AI, while in some ways resembling the chance operations and recombinatorial procedures of the earlier avant-garde expemplified by John Cage, do not in fact resemble the actual facts of his work. Cage did his chance operations in a slowed down way. His use of the I Ching was part of a contemplative artistic process, not just punching in commands at a whim. As such, until we can regain our composure and pull ourselves away from the immersive grip of the hyperattentive state induced by the constant influx of media and data made possible by what Cascone has often called McGovCorp, it will remain difficult for sophisticated artworks in any medium to find a receptive audience. Like the artist, the audience also needs to be able to open the valve to the unconscious. Digital media in its current incarnation works as a firehose blasting the senses. Overstimulation is part of the issue. To tune in, sometimes the first step isn’t turning on, but turning off. Post-Digital Music (Essays) is available on Silent Records. items.body: To complement her interview in The Wire 512, Slovenian improvising pianist and bandleader Kaja Draksler creates an exclusive Wire mix Kaja Draksler studied jazz at a music-oriented high school in Ljubljana, later enrolling at the Conservatory of Amsterdam. There, her instructor, the British composer Richard Ayres, asked her the simple question,“What do you want to do?”, which set her on a path that would chafe against the jazz orthodoxy. In August Punkt.Vrt. Plastik, her long-running trio with Swedish bassist Petter Eldh and German drummer Christian Lillinger, released their fourth album, Kompress, while another of her groups, matter 100, releases its debut True Or False this October. This exclusive mix, she explains, is “more of a collage, where I mostly take excerpts from different pieces, placing them one after the other, and, at times, one of top of the other. The track selection is a mix of my own music and music I love, with a bit of a focus on piano and voices.” Tracklist Kaja Draksler “Prst, roka, laket” (excerpt) Vaqif Mustafazadə “Bizim Bakı Gecələri” (excerpt) Luciano Berio “A La Femminisca” Christian Lillinger “Poliform” (excerpt) Punkt.Vrt.Plastik “EKV” Vince Staples “Get Paid” New London Chamber Choir & James Wood “Serment” (excerpt) Georges Aperghis “Recitation 10_ left part, 1st version” Nina Simone “Who Am I” Irena Z Tomažin “Rain” (excerpt) Pauline Oliveros “Horse Sings From A Cloud” (excerpt) J Gallus “Mirabile Misterium: De Nativitate Circumcisione Et Epiphania Domini Huelgas Ensemble” matter 100 “Rushing Through The Night” (excerpt) Czajka & Puchacz “Wacky Compass” (excerpt(s)) MIA “Sunshowers” (excerpt) Cecil Taylor “Pt 4 Glossalalia” (excerpt) Craig Taborn “Glossolalia” Kaja Draksler Octet “Come See” (excerpt) Andrew Parrot “De Torrente” Judith Berkson “Castle” Ellen Arkbro “For Organ And Brass” (excerpt) matter 100 “Alternating Current” Read Peter Margasak’s full interview with Kaja Draksler in The Wire 512. items.body: Columbus’s Pinta, Niña and Santa María sail through “Delfín del Mundo” alongside pineapples, cockerels, chocolate, tobacco and caipirinhas, a roll call of conquest and tropical produce chanted over a psychedelic cumbia. “Delfín del Mundo” is the third and final single from Desertropical, the new EP from Dr. Rayo, due in October on Costa Rican label Lácteo Cósmico. The project belongs to Red Jesus, a Chilean-Mexican percussionist and producer who spent 2014 to 2020 on Mexico’s independent circuit. Now based in Madrid, he launched the project with a sold-out night at Moby Dick. Red Jesus made the track with Barzo, the San José-born DJ and producer who runs Lácteo Cósmico and has remixed Janelle Monáe and Erykah Badu. He came to Madrid for a short visit, and the pair recorded most of the instruments live at Dr. Rayo’s base. Barzo then built the electronic production on top of those takes. The earlier singles “Mexicali Tropical” and “Owl on Cocaine” opened big and dramatic, while “Delfín del Mundo” settles into a mid-tempo sway built on a slow-burning bassline, live percussion and a vocal delivered close to a chant. The vocal carries a message of pride in Latin American roots, and the cacao, tobacco and pineapples in the lyric were growing in the Americas long before Columbus’s ships arrived. Desertropical gets a launch party at Madrid’s Siroco at the end of September, with Spanish dates to follow in Seville, Oviedo, Gijón, Logroño and Santander. items.body: Label: Edition Records, 2026 Personnel - Mark Guiliana: drums, percussion, electronics, keyboards, guitar, vocals; Nicholas Semrad: keyboards; Stu Brooks: electric bass (#3), electronics (#2,4,7,8); Tim Lefebvre: electric bass (#2,4,6); Gretchen Parlato: vocals (#4,5); Marley Guiliana: vocals (#5). Mixed feelings arose from listening to Beat Music 2.0 , the synth-infused follow-up to Mark Guiliana’s Grammy-nominated album Beat Music! Beat Music! Beat Music! (Motéma, 2019). Retro and futuristic waves emerge from Guiliana’s compositions, which draw inspiration from early gaming culture and electronic music. Still, the focus here is on human connection and collaboration, as he enlists keyboardist Nicholas Semrad, bassist Tim Lefebvre, vocalist Gretchen Parlato, and Stu Brooks on electronics. The opener, “ B.ANG ”, excavates retro electronic music through glitchy synth ostinatos that march alongside the harmonic progression, along with a mix of ambient undercurrents and Gary Numan-style electro-rock energy. Although it tests the elasticity of the song’s edges, this piece failed to leave a strong impression on me. “ B.ORN ” and “ W.EST ” are also nothing special, while “ D.RUM ”, with its industrial stomp generating controlled trepidation and Parlato’s vocals highlighting the contrasting ambient-leaning passages, has a little more flair. I did feel a spark on numbers like “ P.LAY ”, whose actively propulsive drumming, together with Lefebvre’s brawny bass fluxes and pedals, is nothing short of gravity-defying, and “ B.EAT ”, whose grooving dub atmosphere morphs into club-dance territory for a while. Brooks, who infuses relevant, to-the-point electronics into the former, switches to electric bass on the latter. Also worth mentioning is “ M.OVE ”, whose danceable techno patterns reminded me of 808 State. Cross-rhythmic tides and dramatic shifts make this one a standout. Guiliana’s passion for what he does is undeniable, yet the prevailing virtues of Beat Music 2.0 come to the fore when the layers adopt a less explicit old-school electronic vibe in favor of more modernistic experimentation. items.body: Macrozones ultimately feels like a succinct collection of lost time capsules, each one preserving a slightly different shade of distant sound, blurred memory, and quiet unease. A sonic pallet worth every minute of our time. Gradually dissolving into oblivion Buffalo, New York-based survey channel continues the pursuit of cyclical ambient electronic connections with five-piece Macrozones, inhabiting what the artist describes as “mirroring the friction between internal compulsion and a search for genuine stillness.” Each piece drifts weightlessly through that tension, shaped by blurred tones, muted rhythms, and distant melodic echoes. Opener “Mask of Continuity” sets things in motion with subtle synth sparks and soft, lingering tones, while “The Integration” draws deeper into darker drone filaments. Loosely excavated pitter-patter beats emerge within solemn “Inner ​Landscape,” giving its hazy textures a faint rhythmic pulse without ever disturbing their stillness. Penultimate track “Ruinenlust” unfolds as a translucent ambient electronic tapestry, moving through nostalgic, Boards of Canada-laden tropes with a beautifully faded quality. Closing piece “Voice Guiding” carries on this hauntological thread, gradually dissolving into oblivion as distortion and fog-like atmosphere and conversation leaves behind a sense of something half-remembered. Macrozones ultimately feels like a succinct collection of lost time capsules, each one preserving a slightly different shade of distant sound, blurred memory, and quiet unease. A sonic pallet worth every minute of our time. Macrozones is available on Bandcamp. items.body: A centuries-old devotional song from Morocco’s Gnawa repertoire, “M’Bara Meskin” tells of poor M’Bara, left outside the shrine in torn clothes to brew his tea from leaves others have thrown away. Inside, the Sidi and the Lalla, Moroccan honorifics for a gentleman and a lady, sip theirs in their slippers. Sydney-born multi-instrumentalist Julian Belbachir has rebuilt it on reggae and dub, keeping the vocal in Moroccan Arabic, from sessions in Morocco, Mali, Australia, Canada and Jamaica. Belbachir was born to a Moroccan father and an Australian mother and grew up in Surry Hills and Redfern, where he started on West African drums at five under griots and master drummers from Sydney’s African diaspora. He went on to study percussion and instrument-making in Guinea, Senegal, Mali and Morocco, and plays the kamele n’goni, the harp-lute of Mali’s Wassoulou region. From 2013 to 2022 he drummed for the Australian Indigenous dub band OKA, and after the death of its founder, Stuart “Boga” Fergie, he went solo with his 2022 debut album, Babdoukkala. Gnawa music was carried into Morocco by West Africans brought north across the Sahara, many of them enslaved, and the personnel on his forthcoming album, The Golden Light, follow the same route: more than 30 musicians from Mali and Morocco, among them Moussa Diakite, lead guitarist for Salif Keita. “M’Bara Meskin” came out on 11 September as its first single, with the album due in February 2027. Belbachir hears the song as a portrait of “the hardships musicians face in their daily lives“. The video, shot on Super 8 over two trips to Essaouira three years apart, follows his collaborators through rehearsals, recording sessions and time with their community in the Atlantic port best known for its annual Gnawa festival. items._cn_summary: 这首歌源自摩洛哥格纳瓦传统宗教歌曲，讲述穷人M'Bara衣衫褴褛在神殿外用他人丢弃的茶叶泡茶的故事，而殿内的贵人却在拖鞋旁优雅品茗。澳大利亚出生的多乐器演奏家Julian Belbachir将其重构于雷鬼与dub的骨架之上，保留了摩洛哥阿拉伯语的人声。他在摩洛哥、马里、澳大利亚、加拿大和牙买加完成录音，召集了三十余位来自马里与摩洛哥的乐手参与其即将发行的专辑《The Golden Light》，其中包括Salif Keita的首席吉他手Moussa Diakite。Belbachir将这首作品视为音乐人在日常生活中所承受艰辛的写照。MV以Super 8胶片拍摄于索维拉，记录了排练、录音以及与当地社群共处的时刻。作为一首跨越撒哈拉南北、融合西非传统与现代律动的跨界作品，它展现了跨大陆音乐协作的丰富层次。

items.body: Adrian Utley, the guitarist and co-founder of Portishead, has reworked “Étude Op. 25 No. 12” from Polish composer Mariusz Szypura’s “Chopin Residue,” a project that removes the piano entirely from nine of Frédéric Chopin’s best-known piano pieces. The rework arrives today as the latest single from the double album, which Cleopatra Records brings to CD and double vinyl on 16 October; an immersive Blu-ray edition mixed in Dolby Atmos is already available. Chopin Residue by Mariusz Szypura Szypura said working with Utley was a long-held ambition: “Adrian and Portishead are among my favourite musicians. The sound, the approach to making music, the search for unobvious and lo-fi textures, all of it had an enormous influence on me.” Szypura kept the harmonic structure and phrasing of Chopin’s originals while stripping out the instrument itself. He described the decision as a matter of respect rather than provocation: “I rejected the piano immediately. […] I decided Chopin didn’t deserve such profanation. I could only approach this material through the prism of my own sensitivity, harmony, and deconstruction. So I took the piano out. […] The piano was the delivery system, not the content.” Adrian Utley’s rework of ‘Étude Op. 25 No. 12’ “Chopin Residue” splits into two discs: “Deconstructions,” on which Szypura rebuilds nine Chopin pieces with a cast including Lee Ranaldo (Sonic Youth), David Pajo (Slint), Joey Waronker, Gail Ann Dorsey, John McEntire (Tortoise) and John Stanier (Battles), and “Reworks,” on which a second group of artists takes those deconstructed recordings further from the source. Utley’s “Étude Op. 25 No. 12” opens the second disc alongside reworks by Fennesz, Matthew Herbert, Masayoshi Fujita, Sean O’Hagan, Jim O’Rourke, Christine Ott, Benoît Pioulard and Abul Mogard. Szypura described the difference between the two discs directly: “‘Étude Op. 25 No. 12’ is Adrian’s reconstruction, not my piece with his guitar on top. That is the principle of the whole second disc: nine artists, nine rebuilds, each in their own language.” The two discs are designed to be played together as well as separately, an idea that extends into the Blu-ray edition’s Dolby Atmos mix. Szypura said: “They were built to overlap. […] In stereo you hear an arrangement. In Atmos you’re inside the harmonic space with the piano missing from the middle of it. […] That’s not a format upgrade, it’s closer to what the piece was always trying to do.” “Chopin Residue” gets its UK stage premiere at London’s Cadogan Hall on 26 September, as part of the Polish Jazz Festival. Its packaging has also picked up a Bronze A’ Design Award and a Red Dot Award. About Adrian Utley and Mariusz Szypura Adrian Utley was born in Northampton in 1957 and moved to Bristol in the mid-1980s, where he played guitar in touring bands led by jazz organist Big John Patton and drummer Art Blakey’s Jazz Messengers. He co-founded Portishead in Bristol in 1991 with Geoff Barrow and Beth Gibbons, co-producing and playing on the band’s albums “Dummy” (1994), “Portishead” (1997) and “Third” (2008). Outside the band, Utley has recorded and toured with Marianne Faithfull, Jeff Beck and Will Gregory of Goldfrapp, leads his own ensemble Adrian Utley’s Guitar Orchestra, and has scored film and audio work with director Nic Roeg, naturalist David Attenborough and Britain’s National Trust. Mariusz Szypura is a composer, producer and visual artist born in 1972 and based in Warsaw. He started out in the early 1990s in the Poznań rock band Happy Pills before founding his main recording project, Silver Rocket, releasing five albums including “Infinity Fidelity,” a Dolby Atmos record that won Gold for Music/Film Cover at the 2025 European Design Awards. His installation work includes “in:human” at the Centre for Contemporary Art Ujazdowski Castle in Warsaw (2024) and “êkhos” at Lincoln Center during Unsound Festival New York (2024). “Chopin Residue” grew out of that installation practice: Szypura first released the album digitally and on 2LP, 2CD, 2MC and Blu-ray through his own Black Element Label in Warsaw on 28 November 2025, alongside gallery and listening events in New York, Osaka, Los Angeles and Warsaw. Cleopatra Records now extends that release internationally, bringing “Chopin Residue” to CD and double vinyl on 16 October 2026 while the Blu-ray Immersive Edition remains available from its earlier release.

items.album: Faded Pulse Finds Solace in the Past on Ethereal Goth Album “Elysia”
items.excerpt: Hear a voice call through the trees Leave this dying world behind Come along and follow me To the meadows of our minds A good fairy tale knows that beauty can get you into trouble, and that an invitation to dance may come with terms and conditions nobody bothered to explain. For Washington, D.C.’s Faeryn Johnson, the musician behind Faded Pulse, that uneasy invitation opens onto Elysia, a second album where ethereal wave, goth, folk, and dream pop meet the romantic imagination of medieval poetry
items.body: Hear a voice call through the trees Leave this dying world behind Come along and follow me To the meadows of our minds A good fairy tale knows that beauty can get you into trouble, and that an invitation to dance may come with terms and conditions nobody bothered to explain. For Washington, D.C.’s Faeryn Johnson, the musician behind Faded Pulse, that uneasy invitation opens onto Elysia, a second album where ethereal wave, goth, folk, and dream pop meet the romantic imagination of medieval poetry and Victorian painting. Acoustic guitars, hammered dulcimer, electric bass, and ambient synthesizers accompany water spirits, waiting maidens, and woodland gatherings whose hosts have questionable intentions. The route here runs through the synthpop of 2025’s Submission and the more ethereal leanings of that year’s Fallen EP, with a decisive turn taken while watching Monica Richards perform with Strange Boutique in Washington. Johnson’s affection for the 1990s Projekt catalogue supplies another set of coordinates: Lycia, Love Spirals Downwards, Black Tape for a Blue Girl, and Unto Ashes sit alongside the folk of Pentangle and Donovan. There is a generous curiosity at work, the kind that can find room for both a Slowdive bassline and a William Morris poem without making either feel like an unlikely guest. Johnson’s background in art history gives Elysia a visual life as rich as its musical references. Waterhouse’s paintings, the Arts and Crafts movement, and Art Nouveau belong to the same imaginative world as thrifted velvet, medieval dress, and an old copy of Tennyson found in an antique shop. Beneath the finery lie practical questions about courage, community, and how to remain attentive to the living world. This gathering of fairies may be perilous, but the hope is that listeners return from it with a renewed appetite for their own lives. We spoke with Johnson about the records that opened those doors, the literature and paintings behind Elysia, and the enduring possibilities of ethereal music, from a hammered dulcimer to a dream performance among the art and architecture of the Cloisters. Before Faded Pulse, what first opened the door to the Gothic imagination for you? Was there a particular record, book, painting, or encounter that made you feel you had found somewhere you belonged? Faded Pulse: I started getting into the gothic scene when I was around 14 years old, and at that time my most essential record was The Cure’s Pornography. I loved the dense, almost psychedelic sound of the album. I’ve probably overplayed that record way too much at that age. Yet it really cemented my love for atmosphere and dense sound design. Robert Smith’s honest and vulnerable lyricism made me feel so seen and got me through so much. Between Submission, Fallen, and Elysia, your music has moved further into folk and ethereal wave. What was happening in your life and listening habits that encouraged that change, and what could you express through these arrangements that you hadn’t explored before? Faded Pulse: When I first started “Submission” around 2022, I was very much into the New Wave and Synthpop sounds of the 80s, and that really shows on that album, although my listening has always been more eclectic. One big influence on Elysia was psych and folk of the 60s and 70s, particularly bands like Pentangle; their album Solomon’s Seal was super influential on me, especially songs like “Willy O’Winsbury”. Donovan was another big influence; you can really hear it on songs like “Will Thy Heart Be True,” where I go for a more folky, ballad-type song. I have always had a huge love for the 90’s ethereal scene. The moment I knew I wanted to move sonically towards that was when I saw Strange Boutique live at the Black Cat in D.C. in 2025. Seeing Monica Richards on stage and hearing the music live was really a light-bulb moment for me. Ethereal allows me to experiment more with unusual instrumentation and also lets the music take people to another world. Although I enjoyed making synth pop, here I can play with classical, folk, ambient, and even more rock-oriented structures. It’s so much more playful and freeing. I feel like Faded Pulse would have been a perfect fit for Projekt Festival, especially the 1997 edition. How were you first introduced to the label and its artists, and was there a particular band or record that sparked your affinity for that strain of ethereal music? Faded Pulse: Projekt has a special place in my heart and is probably one of my favorite labels ever. My essential four artists from the record label are Black Tape, Lycia, Love Spirals, and Unto Ashes. Black Tape for a Blue Girl’s “Remnants of a Deeper Purity” is one of my all-time favs; it is a masterpiece in its own right in sound design and atmosphere, and it’s both deeply haunting and romantic. I feel like Love Spirals Downwards Idylls is glaringly obvious as one of the influences on Elysia, and I feel it is their most essential record. It’s hard for me to choose a Lycia album because they’re my favorite band on the label, but if I had to choose, it would be “A Day in the Stark Corner”. It’s equal parts dreamy, cold, and bleak. Unto Ashes serves everything I look for in a band: medieval instruments and sounds, folk and darkwave synths. I feel like their album “Empty into white” is so sonically rich and put together, sinister yet dreamy. I’m not sure how I even stumbled on the label, which feels fitting, like it came to me almost in a dream; it is the most influential group of artists for me. There’s something about Elysia that feels entirely at home in the pages of Propaganda or Carpe Noctem. What feels special to you about the Gothic culture of the ’90s, and how have you encountered that period through its music, magazines, photography, and fashion? Faded Pulse: Funnily enough, I own an issue of Propaganda, No. 22, and I wanna say it’s from 1994-1996. I have very fond memories of reading Propaganda magazines in high school on the Internet Archive. I am a historian at heart and love to learn everything I can about culture, music, and fashions of any time period I study. The 90’s, to me, feel somehow criminally underrated, even though it was when the gothic scene was at its peak and fully found itself and diversified into many different interests. I feel the worship of the 80s has caused people to overlook how creative the scene was in the 90s. Even now, somehow darkwave from the 90s is still more experimental and fresh than the very 80s-oriented sounds we get today. As for the fashion, I would study a lot of the pictures on Pinterest from magazines, club shoots, or people’s personal uploads, and when I went thrifting, I would look for similar items. PVC, Satins, Silks, and Velvet are all mainstays in my closet thanks to the 90s, haha. “Meadow of My Mind” and “Upon the Heavens” feel like a bridge between Cocteau Twins and the more romantic corners of the Projekt catalogue. How do you approach the relationship between voice and guitar in these songs, especially when both seem capable of carrying the melody or dissolving into one another? Faded Pulse: Much like the bands before me, I kind of treat the voice as just another instrument. When recording a lot of these songs, I wanted the guitar and voice to mesh well. In meadow of my mind, the voice and guitar switch throughout the song, giving them space to drive the song along without clashing. In “Meadow of My Mind,” you sing, “Leave this dying world behind,” yet you’ve described Elysia as something beyond escapism. What does that inner refuge make possible for you, and what do you hope listeners bring back from it into their everyday lives? Faded Pulse: To me, “Meadow of my Mind” is about the love of nature, to put it plainly. When listeners “Leave the realm of Elysia,” I want people to bring that sort of magic into their everyday lives. Whether that be getting involved in their local communities, making art, or reading poetry. Whatever it is that makes you feel connected to the world around you. “Upon the Heavens” uses the language of prayer, reaching toward a divine presence and asking to be heard and healed. What is your relationship with that devotional language, and how did you arrive at the kind of sacred experience you wanted the song to convey? Faded Pulse: To me, music is very spiritual, and I definitely wanted Upon the Heavens to emulate that in some way. It’s not a song devoted to a particular deity or religion, but it is about reaching out and feeling something greater. I feel this all the time through music, when I listen to a song that just makes me float away or feel high on euphoria. I mean, historically speaking, music is how people connect to the otherworld and is used in ritual, even though it is now far removed from its sacred roots. Music still feels deeply spiritual and otherworldly, and I think that’s truly what the song conveys. “Lamia’s Kiss” brings to mind Dead Can Dance’s exploration of musical traditions beyond rock, with an experimental quality that feels ancient and unfamiliar at once. Which specific traditions, recordings, or instruments informed it, and how did you develop its musical character? Faded Pulse: The sounds of the Middle East and the Mediterranean very much inspire Lamia’s kiss. A lot of the bands I liked, like Lovespirals, DCD, and Rajna, had eastern influence in their music, so it kinda bled into my consciousness. Rather than writing cliched lyrics about her as a figure, I wanted the song to emulate what it would feel like to be caught in her hypnotic gaze, to be pulled in. Instrumentally, I wanted the Dulcimer to be the lead on the song, which I feel really harnesses that archaic, almost ancient vibe that I wanted the song to have. I also grew up in Asia for a short time. I do think it had a musical effect on me, and it seems only natural that an experience like that would creep into my music in some way. What first drew you to Lamia as a figure? Did you come to her through mythology, Keats’s poem, a painting, or another interpretation, and what interests you about the meeting of beauty, desire, and danger in her story? Faded Pulse: It’s a little bit of all of that. Keats’s poem is definitely an inspo, as is Waterhouse’s iconic painting. I am also a Lilith and Hecate Devotee; the lamia is associated with both, so it’s almost devotional. I also love serpentine imagery and symbolism, as well as the figure of the femme fatale, so it is essentially a collage of many different ideas and feelings. “Fair Lady in Gold” has a baroque richness and a medieval atmosphere, particularly in the bright, struck-string sound that suggests a hammered dulcimer. How did you build that arrangement, and who—or what—is the lady at its center? Faded Pulse: For “Fair Lady in Gold,” I knew I wanted to have a few instrumental tracks on the album. The main instruments here are my Dusty Strings hammered dulcimer and my Korg Minilogue for ambient synths. There is no single song as an influence; rather, months and weeks of studying and listening to music from the Renaissance and medieval period that shaped this song. When I first started writing “The Lady in Gold,” I was envisioning Cordelia from King Lear in a painting by Edwin Austin Abbey. Although her gown is yellow, it is not even close to gold, haha. However, a woman with a golden pooling Bliaut gown was what I was envisioning when creating the song, so the name kinda stuck. “Summerland” seems to occupy a meeting place between Dead Can Dance and Cocteau Twins, while its lyrics describe being drawn into a fairy gathering. How welcoming did you want that invitation to feel, and how much uncertainty or danger belongs within its beauty? Faded Pulse: Summerland is definitely a song where I wanted the listener to be taken away by the fae, where it’s both exhilarating and panic-inducing. To be led away and dancing with beings who look human, yet there is something quite off about them, and strange things happen around them. I wanted to evoke the same feelings I had reading Irish fairy tales, where the stories of the fae are both wondrous and terrifying in equal measure. I think it’s a great metaphor for nature itself. Beautiful yet dangerous. “Undine” recalls the dreamier side of 4AD, alongside Faith and the Muse and Lycia, but its bassline and guitar flourishes also make ethereal wave’s goth and post-punk origins audible. How conscious are you of that connection when writing, and what does the bass allow you to do beneath such expansive arrangements? Faded Pulse: The bassline for Undine was heavily inspired by the bassline in Slowdive’s “Ballad of Sister Sue.” I knew I wanted this waltzy song where the bass carried much of the song’s sway. To me, the bass here is the most important; it just wouldn’t sound the same with a synth bass. It really gives the song that romantic rhythm I feel it needed. The words to “Undine” address the water-born figure directly, questioning her lover’s constancy and encouraging her to voice her feelings. Whose voice did you imagine addressing her, and what did you want your interpretation to reveal about her beyond the familiar tragedy? Faded Pulse: With Undine, I knew I really wanted to do a melancholic song about a siren, where the song itself is almost like a lament, where it feels like a spell is being cast onto the listener. The voice that carries the song is part third-person narrator and part Undine’s voice. The Chorus is nonsensical and is a made-up language, but it is Undine casting her spell, hoping and praying to keep Huldbrand’s love. The third-person voice beckons Undine to own her sadness and heartbreak to sing what’s in her heart and drown in her tears, tragically ending the knight’s life, but also having the strength to embrace her own emotions of love and betrayal. “Will Thy Heart Be True?” has the feel of an ethereal folk ballad, with its knight, waiting maiden, and tests of courage. Which Arthurian or medieval texts informed the song, and what does the question of remaining true mean to you personally? Faded Pulse: I think the concept of knight and maiden came to me through William Morris’s poem “Two Red Roses Across the Moon.” Although I’ve been a fan of Morris for a few years, I first heard of it when I visited the American Arts and Crafts Museum and saw a mural depicting the maiden from the poem waiting for her knight, who was off at war. Although I love the stereotypical depiction of the medieval romance trope, the song really isn’t solely about that. It is about staying strong during dark times and finding the courage to go on, which I feel is extremely relevant. Now, the question “Will Thy Heart be True?” is really asking, “Do you have the strength to keep fighting the good fight?” even when it seems hopeless. Your influences include Romantic literature, medieval poetry, and Victorian fairy tales. Which writers have most shaped your imagination—Keats, Christina Rossetti, William Morris, or perhaps someone less immediately expected? Could you take us through one passage or story that found its way into Elysia? Faded Pulse: One of my biggest influences was Alfred Lord Tennyson’s Idylls of the King, a book I thrifted in an antique shop. It features a poetic retelling of Arthurian legends, and although none of its stories made it into Elysia, I knew I wanted Elysia to evoke the feeling of magic, mystery, and romance that the book gave me. Poems like Coleridge’s Christabel and Keats’s La Belle Dame sans Merci were hugely influential as well. Keats’s story of the Faery woman leading the gullible knight astray was definitely an inspo for Summerland. Your art-history background brings the Pre-Raphaelites, Art Nouveau, and the Arts and Crafts movement into the album’s conception. Is there a particular work by an artist such as Burne-Jones, Waterhouse, or Mucha that you could place beside one of these songs and explain the connection? Faded Pulse: Rather than a single painting, artwork, or artist, Elysia sounds like the movements as a whole and what they were trying to achieve. To me, I want people to look at any art from any of those movements and instantly think of a song from Elysia. But if I had to choose an image to associate with the album, I would choose Waterhouse’s Ophelia, as it was one of the few paintings that made me think, “I want to make music that emulates how this painting feels.” Your photographs feature flowing robes, a circlet, a sword, woodland, and Gothic architecture. Which historical garments, designers, films, or figures inform your sense of dress, and how much of that appearance comes from making or adapting things yourself? Faded Pulse: A lot of Elysia’s costumes are based on a combination of different things. For me, it was studying fashion history throughout the Middle Ages, a lot of the Medieval revival clothing coming out of the goth scene in the 90s, and of course, fantasy films like The Lord of the Rings (Particularly the elves). Photographs of Lisa Hammer and Monica Richards in the 90s and 00s were also influential on me. To me, Lisa is a modern Pre-Raphaelite fashion icon, and I definitely wanted to emulate that for Elysia. A lot of the wardrobe for the photos was thrifted or modified to achieve that vibe. What do you think made ethereal wave such a natural home for medieval romance, folklore, and mystery? Within your own music, what do those older forms of imagination allow you to say about love, longing, or belonging in the present? Faded Pulse: I think there’s something very classic about medieval folklore and stories. They feel very timeless with their usage of romance, bravery, and fighting for something you think is worth fighting for. They capture what it means to be human and to be alive. I think Medieval and Ethereal are so drawn to each other because they both have a sense of whimsy and otherworldliness. I think this element of fantasy is so unique to Ethereal outside of the other core genres of the gothic scene. With ethereal, I can weave stories and ambiance that fully immerse the listener into the world I want to create, and I think that’s why fairytales and ethereal go so well together; it’s a perfect mesh of storytelling and sonic immersion. An enduring part of the Gothic imagination is its embrace of mystery and the wonders of nature. Do you feel that connection is more important than ever in this age of AI, and what role can music play in keeping that sense of wonder alive? Faded Pulse: I think music is more important now than ever in the age of AI. It requires you to engage no matter what, to let go, sit down, and spend your time listening, to feel something. I think music is intrinsically human, and I feel that when people go out to clubs or venues for shows and connect with those around them, it really helps them disconnect from the haze of being online all the time and brings them into the present. There is something magical about watching people perform and bring something out of you. That is something that AI could never replace. If you could present Elysia in a setting entirely of your choosing, what would a Faded Pulse performance look and feel like? How would the space, clothing, and instrumentation help bring listeners into these songs, and what would you want them to feel when they stepped outside again? Faded Pulse: I think two of my dream performance locations would be a medieval ruin or within the Met Cloisters Museum in New York. I feel like being surrounded by actual medieval art and architecture would really set the ambiance. One thing I’ve heard of is that bands in the 90s would have incense burning on stage. I don’t know how true that is, and of course, venues would never allow that now, but I think something like frankincense or sandalwood would be my chosen scent, and I feel like playing with multiple senses would really elevate the performance. For dress, I think it would be cool to have a lot of the new-agey medieval revival looks from the nineties that were popular in the scene, and, of course, I would encourage everyone to participate in dressing up if they so choose. For me, I want the audience to feel like they entered another realm, dreamy and untethered, and when they leave, feeling like they had a spiritual awakening.§ For all its mythic tales of knights, faeries, and enchanted waters, Elysia is an album that keeps returning to the ordinary work of being present: listening closely, making something, finding courage, and spending time with other people. Johnson’s ideal audience might gather in velvet beneath medieval arches, but the invitation extends well beyond that imagined evening. There is room for wonder in a borrowed book, a local show, or an afternoon among the trees, and Faded Pulse offers plenty of reasons to make room for it. Faded Pulse’s Elysia is out now. Listen to the album below and order here. items.body: As Solid opens its gates, the music takes a single step forward before lifting off. A nascent, endlessly-echoing piano joins a grounded bass – the only part of the music that touches the ground at all – and an airy, washed-out progression enters, too, blossoming into something like a spring breeze. Swirling in light, yogurt-like textures and a playground spirit, sustaining itself and imbued with a fulfilling light, ‘Stones’ is the kindest of openers from Poland’s ambient duo, Bojanek & Michalowski. Things open up even more as the music begins to shape itself, resembling something like a mystical temple which reveals itself to only a select few. The electric guitar bends the atmosphere, shaping it by way of sonic architecture into a towering figure composed out of monolithic distortion and frayed melodies; a statue carving out the face of a God. The guitar rises slowly, gaining momentum as a rolling wave will as it approaches the shore before reaching the point of no return. It then breaks itself, collapsing like the dusty, sand-strewn stone that it is, an ancient rock that can no longer stand. This is where the track’s power lies: in its breaking. The distortion climbs, morphing into the indiscernible roaring of insectile static. It both washes and stains. The music rises up to titanic heights, and this is indicative of the track naming – monoliths, pillars, statues, sculptures. Even the greatest masterpiece must begin with a single stroke, and each journey must begin with a single step. Likewise, the opening note is the alpha and the omega, the first stone at the base of this perfectly-aligned pyramid; habitually repeating, but turning silence into sound and a Sahara drought into an overflowing oasis. At some level, the music is burning in a spell of torturous heat. Temperature-wise,Solid summons up the merciless spike of July or August, but it’s a dry heat, and not a humid, shirt-sticking suffocation. These pillars stand tall and proud. Even during the clashing of tribal drums, the music remains ambient and expansive enough, despite the dog-lead of repetition. But it acts both ways: one person may think of the bass as a restraint, but the bassline can also be a guide, a map back to camp via the predictability of its looping phrase. Popular music is built on anticipation, but it exists in ambient, too – usually in the form of traditional song, with examples being the vocal-heavy music of Julianna Barwick or Alicia Merz. This anticipation and release, this question and answer, can also be found in a loop, albeit lacking a proper resolution because of its repetition. Solid is energetic ambient, the kind that makes you feel alive instead of dosing it up on sleeping pills. Altitude is everywhere in the record. The flight attendant on ‘Figures’ asks passengers to put their seat belts on as the descent begins, but the reverb-soaked, cloud-wispy guitar chords are more like fluttering feathers or falling autumn leaves after the death of summer, while Jacaszek’s remix glides through cut-up pads and skimmers over soft and thin beats. Have a nice flight… www.ncoded.pl
items._cn_summary: 波兰双人组合Bojanek & Michalowski的专辑《Solid》以环境音乐为基底，却在编排上展现出实验性的张力。开场曲目' Stones'从一架回荡不绝的钢琴与低沉的贝斯线起步，吉他音色逐渐扭曲堆叠，化作巨型失真雕塑般的声响建筑，最终在崩塌中释放能量。专辑贯穿部落鼓击、循环乐句与回声弥漫的和弦进行，在重复与预期中寻找张力。乐评将其比作沙漠绿洲——干燥而炽热，兼具高度与广度。整体氛围被形容为充满活力的环境音乐，既具仪式感又不失冥想特质，电吉他与电子纹理交织出高耸的音场结构。评论文笔充满建筑与自然意象的隐喻，强调音乐在破坏瞬间所蕴含的力量。

items.body: By Nickolas Mohanna and Olli Aarni This April, Preservation have added two new releases to their catalogue – Mantis by Brooklyn-based musician Nickolas Mohanna and Muovia by Finland’s Olli Aarni. Nickolas Mohanna primarily works within synth modulation, but the New York musician adds a generous range of acoustic instruments to his music, nestling beside and behind the synths. Zithers, a bowed acoustic guitar, cymbals and bells are all featured, as are various objects found on the streets of New York. And New York City breathes through and out of the music; the synths are busy and hustling, every synth a new avenue or street to explore. They diverge at the end of the block, snaking around the corners. Traffic lights stop and start, pulsing in and out; walk, don’t walk. The afternoon stretches out before the music, its generally bright sound glinting in the weak sun, its sky muted and made pale by heavy, elephantine clouds. The synths start to take shape, and like a subway train they roll through the city at quicker (although they’re not exactly fierce or burning) speeds. When the other instruments enter the mix the synths drop out, leaving a swirling vortex behind. The other tones and timbres slowly inflate to fill the sparser vacuum. The synths hang around in the background, though, and they’re never gone for long. The incisive tones are capable of cutting and dividing up the music, but contrasting this, a series of smooth, muted notes breezes out of an afternoon jazz club, softening the track. This doesn’t last long, either. Mantis shifts between the experimental and the ephemerality of daily life, of transitory meditations on mindfulness that are sucked into the beating heart of a thriving, 24/7 city. Bleeding into one another, the tracks lightly rattle with sweeping, cymbal-led interludes and chiming bells reminiscent of far-away gongs specifically used for meditation and daily chanting. They tickle the side of the notes, barely grazing the music. ‘Silver Theme’ has a floating synth that climbs to a decent altitude. The night covers the city as a darker, crackling drone walks underneath the bridge of a tired piano, and the intermittent sounds by the side of the road cover the boroughs in black cloth. Muovia is the Finnish word for ‘plastic’. Similarly, his music has some degree of artificiality to it, lying there in its open, tranquil ocean among the tangled strands of seaweed and the pretty, colour-splashed coral. Inspired by old New Age music tapes, the music’s sensitive skin gently decays, tingling with soft sensations. The aquatic notes gently cascade, but the music’s been polluted by plastics and other debris. As a result, the sound is grainy and well-worn; it churns like the stomach of a whale after it has inadvertently swallowed something that shouldn’t be there. Still, the music is positive and the light tones ripple over the surface of the tape. Its New Age influence comes across beautifully; the music always refreshing the palette, always going into unexplored, exotic areas and discovering new species along the way. Its lighter, watery sound is more expansive, not timid in the slightest. The thirty minutes float serenely by. The decay is a second-by-second process; the same way that the body, after receiving life, slowly decays. Muovia isn’t in danger of becoming obsolete, of fading away. The crackles in the record’s skin wrinkle and tighten. It’s a noticeable creasing, but it’s just a part of the process of ageing, and the crackles actually give the record a feeling of authenticity that contrasts and contradicts the artificial nature of the plastic. Like the lovely, deep warmth of a needle resting on the groove of a vinyl record, this extra layer and its additional texture really is crucial to the overall weight and depth of the sound. Split into sides A and B, Muovia is a safe, serene cruise across totally tropical seas. www.preservation.com.au

items._cn_summary: Preserve厂牌同期发行两张作品，分别来自布鲁克林音乐人Nickolas Mohanna与芬兰艺术家Olli Aarni。Mohanna以合成器调制为核心，同时引入齐特琴、弓弦吉他、钹、铃铛以及纽约街头拾得物件，合成器声线繁忙而流动，如城市街道般蜿蜒展开，与日常冥想的短暂片段交织。专辑在实验声响与都市白日梦之间来回切换，钹主导的间奏与远方的钟鸣暗示正念与都市节奏的融合。Aarni的作品受老派New Age磁带启发，水声般的音符在磁带质感的颗粒中缓缓流动，以'塑料'为隐喻探讨海洋污染主题——声音颗粒粗粝如被鲸鱼误食的异物，但整体仍保持柔和光亮的底色。两张作品均呈现磁带美学下的环境声响实验，声音处理细腻，情感表达克制而层次分明。

items.body:
After the OĽUN album I reviewed enthusiastically a while back, here’s the next project, again motivated and led by violinist/fiddler/composer Ján Kružliak Jr., continuing the rapprochement, indeed embrace, between Slovakia’s traditional music and its classical music. This time it reconnects the works of classical composers who were inspired by and drew on village musics with those traditional sources and styles.
Three ensembles are involved: the Spectrum Quartett led by Kru�liak with two violins, viola and cello; Nogaband, the traditional-style quartet of fiddles, contra (chording viola) and bass that’s led by fiddler and singer Michal Noga; and the female vocal group Ulijanky, plus guest singer Simona Hulejov�.
The majority of the tracks are interpretations of works by Slovak composer Eugen Suchon (1908-1993), with others from fellow-Slovaks Ilja Zeljenka (1932-2007) and Alexander Moyzes (1906-1984), and Hungarian B�la Bart�k (1881-1945) who did a lot of his very detailed collecting of folk music in Slovakia.
In each case the sources - musicians and locations in villages across Slovakia - are credited in the notes, and these arrangements and performances reconnect with the energy and traditional vocal sound of those sources.
In no way is this an orchestra-smoothed thing; this is gutsy, brilliantly played and sung music with all the spirit, skill and technique of traditional music, from players and singers who deeply understand and inhabit it. It’s a glorious piece of work, music to luxuriate in. There’s too much richness to begin to detail, but here’s a dip into a few moments to give the flavor. The tracks all have very long titles detailing their sources, so for brevity’s sake I’ll just give track numbers.

items.body:
According to its founder, Eugene Rodriguez, who also sings and plays on the record, Los Cenzontles is a �musical group and non-profit organization, which I founded over thirty years ago.�  As he continues in the album�s liner notes, the group �has a long history of producing projects exploring Mexico�s deep roots and our connections with various traditions that, so far, have included Irish, Louisiana Creole, Cuban, American cowboy, classical, pop, rock, and blues�, the latest of which is
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
. Los Cenzontles translates to the mockingbird, or, from its Aztec root word, the bird of four hundred voices. This is a fitting name for the range of musical diversity represented here.
With songs sung in Spanish, Hawaiian, and English, the concept traces back to the legacy of Mexican cowboys who travelled from California to the Hawaiian Islands to wrangle the long-horned cattle introduced there in the nineteenth century. They also brought the guitar. The 16 tracks feature old Hawaiian songs with new Spanish lyrics, old Mexican songs with new Hawaiian lyrics, new compositions, and traditional Americana. Yet it is an entirely cohesive musical package held together by dense arrangements of ukuleles, guitars, Mexican harp, and accordion.
Sonny Lim & David Hidalgo
Besides their distinctive voices, the headline artists Taj Mahal and David Hidalgo provide the gravitas and musicianship that their long and distinguished careers have earned. According to the liner notes, they were the catalysts behind the project and facilitated the choice of songs, arrangements, and played a range of instruments. On vocals they are joined by Hawaiian natives Gary Haleamau, Sheldeen Haleamau, Sonny Lim, and long-time Cenzontles member Fabiola Trujillo.
Deportee
To give a taste of the sessions, included before the traditional �Fishin� Blues� is Taj Mahal teaching the musicians how to play it. Sung by David Hildalgo,  the lovely �A Matter of Time� comes from the 1984 album
Will the Wolf Survive
by his most famous project, Los Lobos. Another standout for me, �Navegar� features a slack string guitar solo reminiscent of Duane Eddie and one of many tasty lap steel turns by Sonny Lim. Their interpretation of Woody Guthrie's �Deportee� moves into social commentary, highlighting the cruel realities of being a migrant worker in America.
Vaquero Paniolo
Recorded over five days, mostly live in one room at the Los Cenzontles headquarters in San Pablo, California, including the talents of some of their academy�s students, the recording has real spontaneity to it. Arrangements are stretched by improvisations, sometimes by several different instruments on a single tune. The project also represents a great spirit of cooperation and diversity of language, culture, age, and gender. It includes the inputs of musical legends, seasoned pros, and amateurs. The wonderfully rich and often stereotyped musical cultures of both Mexico and Hawaii are represented here with the authenticity of lived experience.
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
is a worthy addition to Los Cenzontles� important work. Quoting Rodriguez again, �Culture is a fabric within which we are all woven.�

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. Various Artists - L�ve L�ve (Volume1) (Review) Pedro Lima - Maguidala (Review) Ann O'aro - Bleu (Review)

items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online. items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio
